Divergence is an outcome of applying the update, so the estimand counts every attempted fork; restricted to the $693$ of $720$ that did not collapse, CartPole and Walker are unchanged in sign ($-113.4$ and $-82.1$) and Cheetah becomes unresolved ($-3.9$; $[-17.5,+13.0]$). The task is the unit of inference: each contributes $240$ attempted forks over five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions. The ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for a fixed mechanism, allowing triggers to be judged by the updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 'fork ledger' method to evaluate the actual value of individual updates in continual world models by comparing update vs hold continuations under common random numbers, finding that fixed update mechanisms often decrease performance.
AI.motivation: Current continual world model approaches use fixed replay schedules or prediction-error triggers to decide when to update, but neither reveals the true value of individual updates because a single deployment run cannot show how the model would have performed with different parameter decisions.
AI.method: The paper introduces a 'fork ledger' that branches deployment streams at pre-registered decision points into matched update and hold continuations under common random numbers. It records the return difference ΔR = R_update - R_hold to evaluate the actual utility of each update attempt.
AI.result: Always applying one fixed update mechanism lowered return on all three simulated control tasks: CartPole (-144.0), Walker (-82.8), and Cheetah (-18.6). When restricted to the 693 of 720 update attempts that did not collapse (cause divergence), CartPole and Walker remained negative (-113.4 and -82.1) while Cheetah became unresolved (-3.9). The experiments involved 240 attempted forks per task over five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions.
AI.conclusion: The fork ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for fixed update mechanisms, allowing triggers to be judged by the quality of updates they select rather than just by surprise detection. The results show that indiscriminate updating often harms performance, highlighting the need for smarter update selection mechanisms in continual learning.

title: SemVerBench: Benchmarking LLM Comprehension of Version-Constraint Resolution Semantics
comment: Accepted at the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages, 6 tables
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents constantly decide whether a version satisfies a constraint such as ^1.2.3 or >=2.0,<3, yet their grasp of version-constraint semantics has never been measured directly. We introduce SemVerBench, the first benchmark of LLM version-constraint resolution semantics across three ecosystems (npm, PEP 440, Cargo): 240 machine-checkable items with unique answers, built author-neutrally from four balanced sources (each ecosystem's official test suite plus three frontier LLM proposers) and labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluating six frontier models, we find systematic, predictable per-mechanism blind spots: a partial-comparator carry rule (>1.2 means >=1.3.0) traps every model on Cargo (near 60%), and although standard PEP 440 prefix matching is universal, on zero-pad/post-release corner cases GPT-5.1 collapses (0/26) while Claude stays at 97-100% (verified on a 67-item oracle-validated set). Opus significantly outperforms all other models, and Sonnet outperforms the OpenAI models (McNemar). The failures look more like an activation/application gap than a knowledge gap: injecting the rule or a light correct hint recovers most errors, whereas interval decomposition does not, and models are at ceiling on the basic forms of the same rules. An author-stratified analysis finds no statistically significant self-favoritism. Because the task is verifiable and a free, 100%-correct resolver exists, tool delegation reaches ~100%: coding agents should delegate version resolution to a resolver rather than reason about versions in-head.

AI.tldr: SemVerBench is the first benchmark for testing LLMs' understanding of version-constraint semantics across npm, PEP 440, and Cargo ecosystems, revealing systematic blind spots in frontier models that can be fixed by delegating to external resolvers.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents frequently need to understand version constraints (like ^1.2.3 or >=2.0,<3) but their actual grasp of these semantics has never been systematically measured or benchmarked.
AI.method: Created SemVerBench with 240 machine-checkable items across three ecosystems (npm, PEP 440, Cargo) using balanced sources from official test suites and three frontier LLM proposers, validated by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluated six frontier models and tested interventions like rule injection and hinting.
AI.result: Found systematic blind spots: all models fail on Cargo's partial-comparator carry rule (near 60%), GPT-5.1 collapses on PEP 440 zero-pad/post-release cases (0/26) while Claude maintains 97-100%. Opus significantly outperforms others. Failures appear to be activation/application gaps rather than knowledge gaps, as rule injection recovers most errors but interval decomposition does not. No significant self-favoritism found.
AI.conclusion: Since 100%-correct resolvers exist and failures are systematic, LLM coding agents should delegate version resolution to external tools rather than attempting to reason about versions internally, achieving near-perfect accuracy through tool delegation.

title: When More Is Not Better: Component Anti-Synergy in a P300 Speller
summary: P300 brain-computer interface (BCI) spellers can provide hands-free communication for people with severe motor impairments. Modern pipelines combine multiple individually promising components, often assuming that 'more-is-better'. We tested this assumption using a four-component full-factorial experiment varying the inclusion of Euclidean Alignment (EA), xDAWN spatial filtering, subject calibration, and language model priors on a public P300 dataset. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, repetitions, and information transfer rate (ITR) with mixed-effects models. Results show that the value of components is conditional rather than additive. Calibration was the strongest singular contributor, while EA compensated for its absence in zero-calibration settings. Adding independently useful components could also reduce performance, revealing component anti-synergy. Contrary to conventional wisdom, LM support was not universally beneficial: its effect depends strongly on the strength of the underlying EEG pipeline, while results from a larger LM showed a similar pattern. Together, these findings challenge maximal 'all-on' pipeline design and highlight the value of selecting spatial and language-support components according to the quality of available EEG evidence.

AI.tldr: Components in P300 BCI spellers don't simply add up - their value is conditional, with calibration being most important, and adding more components can sometimes reduce performance due to anti-synergy effects.
AI.motivation: To test the common assumption in P300 BCI speller design that "more-is-better" when combining multiple promising components, challenging the conventional wisdom that simply adding more features always improves performance.
AI.method: Conducted a four-component full-factorial experiment on a public P300 dataset, systematically varying inclusion of: Euclidean Alignment (EA), xDAWN spatial filtering, subject calibration, and language model priors. Evaluated performance using accuracy, repetitions, and information transfer rate (ITR) with mixed-effects models.
AI.result: Component value is conditional rather than additive. Calibration was the strongest singular contributor. EA compensated for lack of calibration in zero-calibration settings. Adding independently useful components could reduce performance (anti-synergy). Language model support wasn't universally beneficial - its effect depends on EEG pipeline strength, with larger LM showing similar patterns.
AI.conclusion: Challenges maximal "all-on" pipeline design for P300 BCIs. Highlights the importance of selecting spatial and language-support components based on available EEG evidence quality, rather than assuming more components always leads to better performance.

title: Can LLMs Follow Medical Expert Logic? A Benchmark for Hierarchical Logical Consistency in Risk-of-Bias Assessment
summary: Evidence-based medicine demands strict logical consistency, yet current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) prioritize superficial label matching over genuine reasoning. We introduce LogiMed-RoB, a benchmark grounded in Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 expert logic, comprising 860 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 14,820 queries. It evaluates models under the Hierarchical Logical Consistency (HLC) framework across four dimensions: Atomic Consistency, Domain Consistency, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness. Experiments on 10 state-of-the-art LLMs reveal a catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: despite the top model reaching 98.88% Atomic Consistency, its end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, with several open-weight architectures plummeting to nearly 0%. We further uncover a systematic evidence-reasoning gap: even when models retrieve high-quality evidence, they fail to deduce correct outcomes in 18.63-40.05% of cases, while Blind Guess Rates reach 48.28%. LogiMed-RoB demonstrates that high outcome accuracy can conceal critical reasoning flaws, underscoring the necessity of white-box logical verification for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: LLMs perform poorly on logical reasoning in medical risk assessment despite high superficial accuracy, revealing catastrophic error compounding and evidence-reasoning gaps.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations focus on superficial label matching rather than genuine logical reasoning consistency, which is crucial for evidence-based medicine and clinical deployment.
AI.method: Introduces LogiMed-RoB benchmark based on Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 logic with 860 RCTs and 14,820 queries, using Hierarchical Logical Consistency framework across four dimensions: Atomic, Domain, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness.
AI.result: Even top models with 98.88% Atomic Consistency collapse to 45.13% end-to-end consistency; open-weight models drop to nearly 0%. Systematic evidence-reasoning gap: models fail to deduce correct outcomes from high-quality evidence 18.63-40.05% of the time, with blind guess rates reaching 48.28%.
AI.conclusion: High outcome accuracy can mask critical reasoning flaws, emphasizing the need for white-box logical verification rather than black-box evaluation for clinical LLM deployment.

title: Phases in a class of associative memories via hidden neurons
summary: Associative memory in the Hopfield network is attractor dynamics in a disordered many-body system, and higher-order and exponential extensions turn its retrieval update into softmax attention. The polynomial and exponential regimes have been analyzed by different methods, with no common architecture in which to ask what fixes the storage scale. In this paper we study the bipartite architecture of Krotov and Hopfield, which we call the class $H$, whose model is fixed by a Lagrangian for each layer, taking the hidden neurons as the order parameter of retrieval. At polynomial load the replica method yields the replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities, and the crosstalk moment is common to Ising and spherical visible neurons, so their differences come from the visible entropy. With a softmax hidden layer the load is exponential, and a copy representation maps the thermodynamics onto random-energy-model counting, with paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases. Heating destabilizes retrieval by quantized reassignments of attention, and typical Gaussian patterns remain metastable at every load. The regimes differ in their crosstalk statistics, central-limit at polynomial load and large-deviation at exponential load, and the class $H$ splits retrieval into two roles, the visible Lagrangian fixing stability and the hidden one the storage scale, two axes that may also guide the design of new Lagrangians.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes associative memory in Hopfield networks through the class H bipartite architecture, showing how polynomial and exponential load regimes differ in crosstalk statistics and how the visible and hidden Lagrangians control stability vs storage capacity.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses of Hopfield networks treat polynomial and exponential storage regimes separately with different methods, lacking a unified architecture to understand what determines storage capacity limits.
AI.method: Studies the class H bipartite architecture (Krotov-Hopfield model) where each layer has a Lagrangian, treating hidden neurons as retrieval order parameters. Uses replica method for polynomial load analysis and copy representation mapping to random-energy-model counting for exponential load.
AI.result: For polynomial load: replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities show crosstalk moments are common to Ising and spherical visible neurons. For exponential load: mapping to random-energy-model reveals paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases. Heating causes quantized reassignments of attention, Gaussian patterns remain metastable.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial and exponential regimes differ fundamentally in crosstalk statistics (central-limit vs large-deviation), and the class H architecture separates retrieval into two roles: visible Lagrangian controls stability while hidden Lagrangian determines storage scale, providing design principles for new Lagrangians.

title: Agentic Share-of-Search: A Multi-Agent AI System for Competitive Decision-Making in LLM-Mediated E-Commerce
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 Decision Science Institute Annual Conference
summary: AI shopping assistants increasingly redirect consumer discovery, creating an urgent need for tools that support seller-side competitive decision-making. We present a multi-agent AI system that automates competitive visibility measurement and root cause diagnosis in LLM-mediated ecommerce. The system introduces Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the decision target, deploys query agents across leading AI platforms, and uses a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend prioritized merchandising interventions. A 100-trial ablation study, presented as a feasibility evaluation of this prototype, shows the agent recovers the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%, 5.5x over chance), rising to 63.9% among high-correlation ablations.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent AI system that measures competitive visibility and diagnoses root causes in AI-mediated ecommerce, showing promising feasibility results in recovering ablated signals.
AI.motivation: AI shopping assistants are redirecting consumer discovery, creating an urgent need for seller-side competitive decision-making tools in LLM-mediated ecommerce environments.
AI.method: The system introduces Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the decision target, deploys query agents across leading AI platforms, and uses a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend prioritized merchandising interventions.
AI.result: In a 100-trial ablation study, the agent recovered the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%, 5.5x over chance), rising to 63.9% among high-correlation ablations, demonstrating feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The prototype multi-agent system shows promising results for automating competitive visibility measurement and root cause diagnosis in AI-mediated ecommerce, addressing the urgent need for seller-side decision support tools.

title: EGGROLL, Unrolled: Understanding and Improving Low-Rank Evolution Strategies at Scale
summary: EGGROLL makes evolution strategies (ES) practical for LLMs by replacing dense Gaussian weight perturbations with low-rank Gaussian products, often of rank one. This choice is computationally attractive but geometrically severe: each rank-one perturbation lies in a zero-volume subset of the ambient matrix space, despite having identity covariance. We characterize the mean EGGROLL update field at finite rank and nonzero perturbation radii, then analyze the error of its finite-population estimator. The population field is obtained by applying an explicit resolvent to the gradient of the objective smoothed by the perturbations. We show that the resolvent can introduce a nonconservative component and can reverse the local stability of an optimum. EGGROLL is nevertheless exact on every quadratic objective at every rank and radius. For smooth objectives, its first local finite-rank correction is $O(σ^2/r)$, and nonasymptotic bounds control the resulting field error under smoothness assumptions. Under a local affine model, rank-one perturbations increase the variance of the gradient estimator by only $\frac{2(m+n+1)}{mn+1}$ relative to dense Gaussian ES, or $0.098\%$ for a $4096\times4096$ matrix. We then introduce LOO-ROLL, a leave-one-out estimator that preserves the finite-rank population field while replacing EGGROLL's two antithetic evaluations per direction by one. At equal evaluation cost, LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks. At matched wall time across ten post-training settings and models up to 8B parameters, LOO-ROLL improves seven outcomes in individual paired tests, with no significant loss. On the GSM8K test set, accuracy increases from $38.1\%$ to $63.0\%$ at 0.6B and from $65.9\%$ to $80.0\%$ at 8B. Transformer measurements recover the predicted finite-rank variance, while the rank comparisons show no reproducible reward-based advantage for rank eight.

AI.tldr: EGGROLL makes evolution strategies practical for LLMs by using low-rank Gaussian perturbations instead of dense ones, reducing computational cost while maintaining performance. LOO-ROLL further improves efficiency with a leave-one-out estimator that halves MSE.
AI.motivation: Evolution strategies (ES) are computationally expensive for large language models due to dense Gaussian weight perturbations. The paper aims to make ES practical for LLMs by reducing computational complexity while maintaining effectiveness.
AI.method: EGGROLL replaces dense Gaussian weight perturbations with low-rank Gaussian products (often rank-one). The authors characterize the mean update field at finite rank, analyze estimator error, and introduce LOO-ROLL - a leave-one-out estimator that reduces antithetic evaluations from two to one per direction.
AI.result: EGGROLL is exact on quadratic objectives at all ranks and radii. For smooth objectives, first local finite-rank correction is O(σ²/r). LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks at equal evaluation cost. GSM8K accuracy improves from 38.1% to 63.0% at 0.6B and 65.9% to 80.0% at 8B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank perturbations make evolution strategies practical for LLMs with minimal performance loss. LOO-ROLL further improves efficiency by reducing antithetic evaluations. The approach enables effective evolution strategies for large-scale models while maintaining strong empirical performance.

title: An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning
summary: With the existing digital mental health tools specifically developed for Western settings, Pakistani students are exposed to a uniquely compounded stress situation in their university that includes academic, financial, familial, and relational stressors, which have become a serious concern for academic and psychological development of students in Pakistani universities. This paper introduces a new, AI-driven and culturally sensitive stress detection and wellness support system that is tailored to the context of Pakistani university students. The system is based on a machine learning model called Random Forest which is trained using a validated student stress data set of 1100 responses on 20 features from psychological, physiological, academic, environmental and social aspects, with an accuracy of 89.09% and a macro F1-score of 0.89, in three stress severity levels. The classification outputs are passed on to an open-source large language model through OpenRouter API, where an appropriately crafted system prompt, culturally aware, gives the model a conversation about wellness, in English, Urdu and Roman Urdu. The second most predictive stress factor in this population identified by feature importance analysis was teacher-student relationship, which is a culturally important stress factor highlighting the need for region-aware mental health systems. Future research will involve primary data collection from students at various academic levels of Pakistani Universities with the validated DASS-21 instrument focusing on the students who are moving from FSc to undergraduate studies, which is a time of being psychologically vulnerable which is under-researched.

AI.tldr: AI-driven culturally sensitive stress detection system for Pakistani university students achieves 89.09% accuracy using Random Forest with LLM-based wellness support in English, Urdu, and Roman Urdu.
AI.motivation: Existing digital mental health tools are developed for Western settings and fail to address the unique compounded stress situation of Pakistani university students, which includes academic, financial, familial, and relational stressors that seriously affect academic and psychological development.
AI.method: The system uses a Random Forest machine learning model trained on a validated dataset of 1100 responses across 20 features from psychological, physiological, academic, environmental, and social aspects. Classification outputs are passed to an open-source LLM via OpenRouter API with a culturally-aware system prompt to generate wellness conversations in English, Urdu, and Roman Urdu.
AI.result: The model achieved 89.09% accuracy and 0.89 macro F1-score in classifying three stress severity levels. Feature importance analysis revealed that teacher-student relationship was the second most predictive stress factor, highlighting the cultural specificity of stressors in Pakistani contexts.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates the effectiveness of culturally-aware AI systems for mental health support in non-Western contexts, with particular emphasis on region-specific stress factors. Future work will involve primary data collection using DASS-21 instrument focusing on the psychologically vulnerable transition period from FSc to undergraduate studies.

title: Thompson Sampling for Non-Monotone Convex Ridge Bandits: Monotonicity Is Not Needed for Polynomial Regret
summary: Bakhtiari, Lattimore and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) proved that Thompson sampling (TS) has Bayesian regret $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ for bandit convex optimisation with convex \emph{monotone} ridge losses $f(x)=\ell(\ip{x}θ)$, and asked whether monotonicity of the link is necessary. We give a qualitative negative answer. For every prior on $[0,1]$-valued, $1$-Lipschitz convex ridge losses with an arbitrary convex, possibly non-monotone, link, and for any fixed measurable selection of minimisers, exact-posterior TS has Bayesian regret $O\big((d+1)^4\sqrt{dn}\,\log(e+nd\max\{1,\diam K\})\big)=\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt n)$. The monotone proof relies on a single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy; we show by an explicit twelve-point configuration that this dichotomy fails for non-monotone links, and replace it by an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for ``uninformative'' configurations. The bound uses a Boolean rounding argument: a $0$-$1$ matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has rank at most $2r-1$. We construct $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses, showing that the cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime, and give a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer that is uniform over fixed measurable selections. Whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence of the monotone case can be retained remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that Thompson sampling achieves Bayesian regret $\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt{n})$ for bandit convex optimization with convex ridge losses, removing the monotonicity assumption from prior work while worsening the dimension dependence from $d^{5/2}$ to $d^{9/2}$.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Bakhtiari, Lattimore and Szepesvári, COLT 2025) proved Thompson sampling has Bayesian regret $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt{n})$ for bandit convex optimization with convex monotone ridge losses. They asked whether monotonicity of the link function is necessary. This paper investigates this open question.
AI.method: The paper replaces the single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy used in the monotone case (which fails for non-monotone links) with an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for "uninformative" configurations. Uses a Boolean rounding argument: a 0-1 matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has rank at most $2r-1$. Constructs $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses and provides a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer that is uniform over fixed measurable selections.
AI.result: For every prior on $[0,1]$-valued, 1-Lipschitz convex ridge losses with arbitrary convex (possibly non-monotone) link, and for any fixed measurable selection of minimizers, exact-posterior Thompson sampling has Bayesian regret $O((d+1)^4\sqrt{dn}\log(e+nd\max\{1,\text{diam }K\})) = \tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt{n})$. The cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime.
AI.conclusion: Monotonicity is not necessary for Thompson sampling to achieve polynomial Bayesian regret in bandit convex optimization, answering the prior work's question in the negative. However, the dimension dependence worsens from $d^{5/2}$ to $d^{9/2}$. Whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence can be retained for non-monotone links remains an open question.

title: CryptoL: Towards Scale Dominance and Physics Constraints Mitigation in Financial Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Cryptocurrency forecasting presents a distinctive combination of extreme cross-asset scale heterogeneity, non-stationary dynamics, and structural dependencies among Open, High, Low, and Close (OHLC) variables. We present CryptoL, a unified framework designed to address these challenges within multivariate time-series forecasting. CryptoL evaluates forecasting error in context-normalized coordinates within the RevIN pipeline, preventing inverse normalization from introducing an additional squared-scale weighting into the MSE objective. We formally characterize this effect through the empirical risk and parameter-gradient geometry, establishing the conditions under which large-scale assets can disproportionately influence shared-model optimization. Beyond loss-space normalization, CryptoL examines channel-independent and channel-dependent normalization for OHLC data, showing that a shared channel-dependent affine transformation preserves candle-order relations that independent channel transformations need not preserve. The framework further incorporates scale-adaptive numerical stabilization to reduce distortions caused by a fixed normalization constant across assets spanning many orders of magnitude, together with a soft feasibility loss that penalizes violations of the defining OHLC inequalities. Experiments across heterogeneous cryptocurrency assets evaluate these components through controlled ablations and demonstrate improvements in forecasting accuracy, training stability, and the frequency of financially valid OHLC predictions relative to the considered baselines. CryptoL therefore provides an integrated approach to scale-balanced optimization, structure-preserving normalization, numerical stabilization, and constraint-aware cryptocurrency forecasting.

AI.tldr: CryptoL is a unified framework for cryptocurrency forecasting that addresses scale heterogeneity and structural OHLC dependencies through context-normalized optimization, scale-adaptive normalization, and constraint-aware modeling.
AI.motivation: Cryptocurrency forecasting presents unique challenges: extreme cross-asset scale heterogeneity (assets spanning many orders of magnitude), non-stationary dynamics, and structural dependencies among OHLC (Open, High, Low, Close) variables. Existing methods can be disproportionately influenced by large-scale assets during optimization.
AI.method: CryptoL uses a unified framework with: 1) Context-normalized coordinates within RevIN pipeline to prevent inverse normalization from introducing squared-scale weighting, 2) Channel-dependent normalization for OHLC data that preserves candle-order relations, 3) Scale-adaptive numerical stabilization to reduce distortions across magnitude-spanning assets, and 4) Soft feasibility loss that penalizes violations of OHLC defining inequalities.
AI.result: Experiments across heterogeneous cryptocurrency assets show improvements in forecasting accuracy, training stability, and the frequency of financially valid OHLC predictions relative to baselines. The framework demonstrates effectiveness through controlled ablations of its components.
AI.conclusion: CryptoL provides an integrated approach to scale-balanced optimization, structure-preserving normalization, numerical stabilization, and constraint-aware cryptocurrency forecasting, effectively addressing the unique challenges of cryptocurrency time-series data.

title: Importance Weighting for Unlabeled-unlabeled Learning under Distribution Shift
summary: Unlabeled-unlabeled (UU) learning allows us to learn a binary classifier from two sets of unlabeled data with different class-priors. It is a general framework because it includes a wide variety of supervised learning such as positive-unlabeled (PU) learning, noisy label learning, and similarity-based learning. Existing UU learning assumes that the test and training distributions have the same class-conditional densities. However, this assumption rarely holds in practice due to distribution shifts. This paper proposes a distribution shift adaptation method for UU learning that uses UU data in the training distribution and a few UU data in the test distribution. The proposed method is based on the importance weighting, which minimizes the test risk by using training data with estimated importance weights. Although existing importance weighting methods cannot handle UU data, we show that it can be done in a principled manner. Thanks to the generality of UU learning, our method can handle various learning problems such as PU and noisy label learning under distribution shift within a single framework while existing methods are usually tailored to a specific problem. Moreover, it does not require any assumption of the shift types such as covariate shift. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Proposes a distribution shift adaptation method for Unlabeled-Unlabeled (UU) learning that handles various supervised learning problems under distribution shift within a single framework using importance weighting.
AI.motivation: Existing UU learning assumes identical training and test distributions, but this rarely holds in practice due to distribution shifts. Current methods cannot handle UU data under distribution shift, and existing solutions are problem-specific rather than general.
AI.method: Uses importance weighting to minimize test risk with training data weighted by estimated importance weights. The method works with UU training data and a few UU test data points, without requiring specific shift type assumptions like covariate shift.
AI.result: The proposed method can handle various learning problems (PU learning, noisy label learning, similarity-based learning) under distribution shift within a single framework, unlike existing specialized methods.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled importance weighting approach for UU learning under distribution shift that is general, requires minimal assumptions, and works across multiple learning problems, demonstrated effective with real-world datasets.

title: A Voice-Interactive Multi-Agent System for Smart Operating Rooms: Architecture Design and Key Technologies
summary: This paper presents SurgicalRoomAgent, a voice-interactive multi-agent system for smart operating rooms based on large language models (LLMs). The system achieves natural language understanding, device control, intraoperative recording, and surgical report generation through a layered architecture comprising a voice interaction pipeline (wake, ASR, turn detection, agent reasoning, TTS) and an agent core (skill registry, task planner, device manager). Three key technologies are investigated: (1) KV Cache prefix warming for low-latency inference, reducing recomputation overhead from approximately 500 ms to tens of milliseconds via byte-level Longest Common Prefix reuse; (2) streaming partial JSON parsing with early parallel task execution, reducing end-to-end latency by approximately 30%; and (3) progressive skill prompt disclosure, which dynamically filters system prompts based on user role, connected devices, and surgical phase to maximize information density within limited context windows. The system is implemented using the Qwen3-27B model with llama.cpp/sglang inference engines. Experimental analysis demonstrates effective operation within a 16,384-token context limit and multi-device parallel control response times meeting OR real-time requirements.

AI.tldr: SurgicalRoomAgent is a voice-controlled LLM-based multi-agent system for operating rooms that achieves real-time device control, surgical recording, and report generation through optimized inference techniques.
AI.motivation: The need for intelligent operating room systems that can understand natural language, control medical devices, record surgical procedures, and generate reports in real-time, requiring low-latency, context-aware interactions suitable for critical surgical environments.
AI.method: A layered architecture with voice interaction pipeline (wake, ASR, turn detection, agent reasoning, TTS) and agent core (skill registry, task planner, device manager). Three optimization techniques: KV Cache prefix warming for low-latency inference, streaming partial JSON parsing with early parallel execution, and progressive skill prompt disclosure based on user role, devices, and surgical phase.
AI.result: Implemented using Qwen3-27B model with llama.cpp/sglang inference engines. The system operates within 16,384-token context limits and achieves multi-device parallel control response times meeting operating room real-time requirements, with KV Cache optimization reducing recomputation from ~500ms to tens of milliseconds and streaming parsing reducing end-to-end latency by ~30%.
AI.conclusion: The SurgicalRoomAgent system demonstrates that LLM-based multi-agent architectures can effectively enable voice-interactive smart operating rooms with real-time performance through careful optimization of inference latency, context management, and parallel execution strategies.

title: Topological Necessities: Mechanism-Invariant Strategic Subgoals for Cross-Embodiment Goal-Conditioned Control
comment: 60 pages total (9-page main text + appendices), 16 figures. Code and data: https://osf.io/wak7u/overview?view_only=70a3d17f63114468a43b2d7a918e47db
summary: Long-horizon goal-conditioned reinforcement learning delegates control to a high-level module that proposes subgoals, but existing subgoals are implicit byproducts of value functions or latent actions, tied to the executor that produced them. We study a different object: a route-conditioned order of unavoidable stages that every successful executor must traverse, recoverable from offline trajectories and belonging to none of them. Its defining properties are topological: an unskippable stage is a separating set that every admissible path must cross, and a loop in free space forces a route choice. We read the two by homology in dimensions 0 and 1 over a transport-weighted carrier built from successful trajectories, yielding an enumerable gate set with shell-level certificates; the certified gates are what we call topological necessities. Certified gates enter the decision loop as a recursive topological gate hierarchy. Under a fixed, isomorphic free space, the object survives executor replacement: gates frozen on PointMaze data transfer without retraining to Ant and Humanoid, attaining the highest Humanoid aggregate under a unified interface (96.1), with +36.0 over a map-privileged reference on the multi-route task (p=1.4e-5); the planner saturates PointMaze (100+/-0) and matches or exceeds the strongest baselines on AntMaze (giant +22.9) and Kitchen (+15.8/+12.6).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces topological necessities - certified gates derived from homology analysis of successful trajectories that serve as unavoidable stages in goal-conditioned RL. These gates transfer across different environments and executors without retraining, improving performance on various robotics tasks.
AI.motivation: Current subgoal methods in long-horizon goal-conditioned RL produce implicit subgoals tied to specific executors. The authors aim to find more fundamental, transferable structures - unavoidable stages that every successful path must traverse, independent of the executor that produced them.
AI.method: Use topological analysis: identify unskippable stages as separating sets (0-dimensional homology) and route choices from loops (1-dimensional homology) over a transport-weighted carrier built from successful trajectories. This yields an enumerable gate set with certificates called "topological necessities." These gates form a recursive topological gate hierarchy for planning.
AI.result: Certified gates transfer across environments and executors without retraining. When trained on PointMaze data, gates transfer to Ant and Humanoid environments, achieving: highest Humanoid aggregate (96.1), +36.0 improvement over map-privileged reference on multi-route task, saturates PointMaze (100±0), and strong performance on AntMaze (+22.9) and Kitchen (+15.8/+12.6) tasks.
AI.conclusion: Topological necessities provide fundamental, transferable structures for goal-conditioned RL that survive executor replacement and enable cross-environment transfer. The approach leverages homology theory to extract unavoidable stages from offline trajectories, creating a unified planning interface that outperforms existing methods across diverse robotics benchmarks.

title: NovGauge: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Diagnosing LLMs' Capability in Paper Novelty Assessment
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in peer review at major AI conferences, yet novelty remains a persistent weak point. Existing benchmarks assess novelty as a single holistic score, making it difficult to diagnose which dimension a model misjudges or whether its evidence is faithful. We present NovGauge, a human-anchored benchmark for fine-grained novelty assessment diagnosis. The benchmark contains 619 paper pairs and 50 multi-paper sets, drawn from two expert sources: ICLR reviewer overlap claims and survey co-citations. Instances are independently labeled along three dimensions: task, problem, and method, capturing application goals, technical challenges, and solution approaches. We propose a cascading diagnostic pipeline that verifies per-dimension correctness, evidence grounding, and logical support. Evaluation of 18 LLMs shows hallucination rates ranging from 0% to 39% across dimensions, and among non-hallucinated correct-positive judgments, over 70% cite evidence fails to logically support the stated reason. The best-performing model, GPT-5.5, achieves 43-72% Verified F1 across dimensions, while most models retain less than half of their raw F1 after faithfulness verification. These results suggest that current LLMs remain far from reliable scientific novelty assessment, particularly when correctness is conditioned on faithful evidence grounding.

AI.tldr: NovGauge is a human-anchored benchmark for fine-grained novelty assessment diagnosis that evaluates LLMs on three dimensions (task, problem, method) and reveals high hallucination rates and evidence faithfulness issues in current models.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assess novelty as a single holistic score, making it difficult to diagnose which dimension a model misjudges or whether its evidence is faithful. There's a need for fine-grained evaluation of LLM performance on scientific novelty assessment in peer review contexts.
AI.method: Created NovGauge benchmark with 619 paper pairs and 50 multi-paper sets from ICLR reviewer overlap claims and survey co-citations. Instances labeled along three dimensions: task, problem, and method. Developed cascading diagnostic pipeline that verifies per-dimension correctness, evidence grounding, and logical support. Evaluated 18 LLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: Hallucination rates ranged from 0% to 39% across dimensions. Among non-hallucinated correct-positive judgments, over 70% had evidence that failed to logically support the stated reason. Best model (GPT-5.5) achieved 43-72% Verified F1 across dimensions, but most models retained less than half their raw F1 after faithfulness verification.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs remain far from reliable scientific novelty assessment, particularly when correctness is conditioned on faithful evidence grounding. The benchmark reveals significant gaps in LLMs' ability to provide faithful, logically supported novelty judgments.

title: T1: Terminal Agent Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Agent usage is shifting toward long-horizon tasks such as coding and scientific discovery, among which terminal tasks are especially important. We introduce T1, a Mixture-of-Experts model of 122B total trained with reinforcement learning, operating a real shell in a cloud sandbox for up to 300+ tool-call turns per task, rewarded by executing each task's own verifier. We provide a comprehensive recipe: First, an aggressively warm-started to stabilize actor-critic training, with a dense process reward scoring trajectories by the absolute number of passing verifiers. Second, stable optimization through TITO construction, training on the exact sampled token identifiers with drift repair at turn boundaries, and rollout routing replay, recording the sampler's per-token expert choices at every MoE layer and replaying them during training. Third, fully out-of-distribution training corpus: isolated seeds and synthesized tasks disjoint from Terminal-Bench 2.1 ensures gains reflect genuine capability transfer over benchmark overfitting. Together, TITO and R3 cut the training-to-inference log-probability difference from 0.021 to 0.013, with exactly aligned zero token drift in the loss region. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, our post-train pipeline raises initial base model from 43.8% to T1 with 64.0% resolved. On Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, T1 reaches 27.9% and surpasses GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1.

AI.tldr: T1 is a 122B Mixture-of-Experts model trained with RL to perform long-horizon terminal tasks by operating real shells in cloud sandboxes, achieving state-of-the-art performance on terminal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agent usage is shifting toward long-horizon tasks like coding and scientific discovery, where terminal tasks are especially important. There's a need for models that can reliably execute complex terminal operations in real environments over extended sequences.
AI.method: Three key innovations: 1) Aggressive warm-starting to stabilize actor-critic training with dense process rewards based on passing verifiers; 2) TITO construction for stable optimization, training on exact sampled tokens with drift repair and rollout routing replay; 3) Fully OOD training corpus from isolated seeds and synthesized tasks disjoint from Terminal-Bench 2.1.
AI.result: T1 achieves 64.0% resolved on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (up from 43.8% base), 27.9% on Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, surpassing GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1. TITO and R3 reduce training-to-inference log-prob difference from 0.021 to 0.013 with zero token drift in loss region.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training pipeline enables reliable long-horizon terminal operation in real shell environments, with gains reflecting genuine capability transfer rather than benchmark overfitting, establishing new state-of-the-art for terminal task agents.

title: Sci-MMR: Benchmarking Multi-Step Evidence-Grounded Scientific Reasoning in Multimodal Agents
summary: Autonomous research agents are increasingly expected to search the literature, analyze experimental evidence, and generate scientific hypotheses. These capabilities require multi-step evidence grounded reasoning that progressively acquires, integrates, and verifies evidence before reaching a conclusion. Existing multimodal benchmarks, however, largely evaluate final-answer accuracy, leaving open whether predictions are actually supported by traceable scientific evidence. We introduce Sci-MMR, a benchmark for multi-step evidence-grounded scientific reasoning built on structured argument graphs linking scientific claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence, and supporting regions. Sci-MMR comprises 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks spanning four scientific disciplines, with an average of nine figure panels per task. Evaluating eight frontier multimodal models, we find that answer accuracy consistently exceeds complete-evidence recovery rate by more than 20%, revealing a substantial gap that answer-only evaluation is structurally unable to capture. Through controlled interventions, we identify two fundamental bottlenecks. First, evidence acquisition: models struggle to extract complete structured evidence from scientific figures, accounting for 57.2% of failures. While cropping tools yield modest gains (+4.5 points), providing gold evidence improves accuracy by up to 37.0 points, indicating difficulty in assembling complete multi-region evidence. Second, evidence integration: models struggle to translate available evidence into correct conclusions, accounting for 31.8% of failures, while even with gold evidence the strongest model achieves only 69.1% accuracy on the hardest tasks. These findings indicate that current answer-centric benchmarks substantially overestimate the evidence-grounded reasoning capabilities of multimodal research agents

AI.tldr: Sci-MMR is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-step evidence-grounded reasoning in multimodal scientific research agents, revealing that current answer-only evaluations substantially overestimate true reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: As autonomous research agents are expected to perform scientific tasks like literature search and hypothesis generation, they require multi-step evidence-grounded reasoning. However, existing multimodal benchmarks only evaluate final-answer accuracy without assessing whether predictions are actually supported by traceable scientific evidence, creating a gap in evaluating true reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce Sci-MMR, a benchmark built on structured argument graphs linking scientific claims, citation-grounded knowledge, visual evidence, and supporting regions. It comprises 235 multi-hop reasoning tasks across four scientific disciplines with an average of nine figure panels per task. They evaluate eight frontier multimodal models using controlled interventions to identify bottlenecks.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals that answer accuracy consistently exceeds complete-evidence recovery rate by more than 20%, showing a substantial gap that answer-only evaluation can't capture. Two fundamental bottlenecks are identified: 1) Evidence acquisition (57.2% of failures) - models struggle to extract complete structured evidence from scientific figures, and 2) Evidence integration (31.8% of failures) - models struggle to translate available evidence into correct conclusions. Even with gold evidence, the strongest model achieves only 69.1% accuracy on hardest tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current answer-centric benchmarks substantially overestimate the evidence-grounded reasoning capabilities of multimodal research agents. The findings highlight critical bottlenecks in evidence acquisition and integration that must be addressed for truly capable scientific AI systems.

title: EMMI: Edge Multi-Modal Intelligence for Communication-Efficient MLLM Inference via Fused Representation Compression
summary: Recent advances in multimodal large language mod- els (MLLMs) have opened new opportunities for edge intelligence by enabling reasoning across heterogeneous sensor modalities, such as vision, text, and telemetry data. However, deploying these capabilities on resource-constrained edge platforms remains challenging due to the substantial computational, memory, and communication demands of modern MLLMs. Rather than transmitting raw sensor observations or partitioning neural networks at intermediate layers, Edge Multi-Modal Intelligence (EMMI) communicates a compact representation between edge devices and server resources, enabling communication-efficient edge MLLM inference. To achieve this, EMMI performs modality-specific encoding, cross-modal representation fusion, and learned compression at the edge, transmitting only a compact latent representation to server-side resources for high-capacity MLLM reasoning. This representation-centric design reduces communication overhead, preserves local data privacy, and provides a fixed-size interface between heterogeneous edge devices and server-side MLLMs. Evaluation on a representative multimodal benchmark demonstrates that EMMI can reduce the communication payload by 32x while maintaining comparable downstream accuracy, resulting in up to a 3.4x reduction in estimated end-to-end inference latency under bandwidth-constrained edge conditions.

AI.tldr: Edge Multi-Modal Intelligence (EMMI) is a communication-efficient framework that enables multimodal large language model inference on edge devices by transmitting compact latent representations instead of raw sensor data or intermediate network layers.
AI.motivation: While multimodal LLMs enable reasoning across sensor modalities for edge intelligence, their deployment on resource-constrained edge platforms is challenging due to high computational, memory, and communication demands. Traditional approaches of transmitting raw sensor data or partitioning neural networks are inefficient for edge environments.
AI.method: EMMI performs three key steps at the edge: 1) modality-specific encoding of sensor data, 2) cross-modal representation fusion, and 3) learned compression to create compact latent representations. These fixed-size representations are then transmitted to server-side MLLMs for reasoning, reducing communication overhead while maintaining privacy.
AI.result: Evaluation on multimodal benchmarks shows EMMI reduces communication payload by 32x while maintaining comparable downstream accuracy. This results in up to 3.4x reduction in estimated end-to-end inference latency under bandwidth-constrained edge conditions.
AI.conclusion: EMMI provides an effective framework for communication-efficient edge MLLM inference by leveraging compact latent representations, addressing key challenges of resource constraints, communication overhead, and data privacy in edge computing environments.

title: AI-Powered Flare Combustion Efficiency Estimation
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Machine Learning and Data Engineering (ICMLDE 2025). 5 pages
summary: Achieving high combustion efficiency in flare stacks is crucial for adhering to regulatory standards and controlling the release of hydrocarbons into the environment. Traditional instruments like gas analyzers and hyperspectral cameras are expensive, fragile, and require frequent calibration, which makes them impractical for remote or budget constrained industrial sites. We propose an innovative solution that combines a lightweight vision-language encoder with a compact multi-layer perceptron to predict combustion efficiency directly from low-cost thermal video footage. The fully trained model is integrated into an easy-to-deploy graphical user interface. This interface overlays predicted combustion efficiency values on each video frame, displays real-time trends in combustion efficiency, shows the distribution of combustion efficiency across all frames in the video, and allows users to export CSV reports. Over a six-month period, the system achieved 99% uptime and required less than 15 minutes of maintenance per week.

AI.tldr: A vision-language model combined with MLP predicts combustion efficiency from thermal video, deployed in a GUI with 99% uptime over six months with minimal maintenance.
AI.motivation: Traditional combustion efficiency monitoring tools (gas analyzers, hyperspectral cameras) are expensive, fragile, require frequent calibration, and are impractical for remote or budget-constrained industrial sites. Need a more practical solution for flare stack monitoring.
AI.method: Proposes an innovative solution combining a lightweight vision-language encoder with a compact multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to predict combustion efficiency directly from low-cost thermal video footage. The trained model is integrated into an easy-to-deploy graphical user interface.
AI.result: The system overlays predicted combustion efficiency values on video frames, displays real-time trends, shows distribution across frames, and allows CSV report export. Achieved 99% uptime over six-month period with less than 15 minutes of weekly maintenance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed solution provides a practical, low-maintenance alternative to traditional expensive instruments for monitoring flare stack combustion efficiency, particularly suitable for remote or budget-constrained industrial sites.

title: The information geometry of large language models is shared, learned, and controllable
summary: Large language models learn similar behaviours, yet it remains unclear what structure they share or how to change one behaviour without disturbing others. The Fisher-Rao geometry of next-token probabilities connects these questions: behaviour determines this geometry up to output-preserving symmetries, whereas activation geometry depends on coordinates. Across transformer, state-space and recurrent models, output geometries agree more strongly than activation geometries, and shared geometry supports semantic-category transfer. Agreement with human word choices increases with predictive accuracy, scale and training, and improves further after model-only calibration. Token probabilities and read-out geometry jointly predict the spectrum and its effective dimension. Controlled language assignments show that geometry follows the language law across architectures. Pretraining corpus statistics predict held-out fact acquisition without recalibration, while randomised experiments show that deeper evidence substantially delays acquisition across every tested architecture and evidence construction. Finally, the geometry prescribes minimum-disturbance local interventions, predicts their relative cost, and supports reusable control: updates learned on donor prompts transfer to unseen prompts while better preserving behaviour on reference prompts than Euclidean control. The same geometric correction improves steering, editing, attribution, dictionary learning and fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Researchers use Fisher-Rao geometry of next-token probabilities to analyze behavioral structure across LLMs, showing shared geometry enables semantic transfer, predicts learning dynamics, and enables minimum-disturbance interventions that transfer across prompts.
AI.motivation: Large language models learn similar behaviors but it's unclear what structure they share and how to modify specific behaviors without affecting others. Understanding the underlying geometric structure could reveal common principles and enable more precise model control.
AI.method: The paper uses Fisher-Rao geometry of next-token probabilities to analyze model behaviors across different architectures (transformer, state-space, recurrent). They study geometry agreement, predict token acquisition, and test controlled interventions through geometric control methods.
AI.result: Output geometries agree more strongly than activation geometries across architectures. Shared geometry supports semantic-category transfer. Geometry predicts token spectra and effective dimensions. Pretraining statistics predict fact acquisition without recalibration. Geometric interventions enable minimum-disturbance control that transfers across prompts while preserving reference behavior.
AI.conclusion: Fisher-Rao geometry provides a powerful framework for understanding and controlling LLM behavior. It reveals shared structural principles across architectures, predicts learning dynamics, and enables precise interventions that minimize disturbance while facilitating transfer across contexts.

title: Predicting Train Delays in Finland Using Machine Learning and Weather Data
comment: 6 pages, 3 Figures, 4 tables, presented at Wireless Europe 2026, Rimini, Italy, June 2026
summary: Reliable railway operations depend increasingly on real-time environmental intelligence delivered through wireless sensor infrastructures, a capability that 6G networks will substantially enhance through integrated sensing and edge computing. Adverse weather, particularly in Arctic regions with extreme temperatures and heavy precipitation, remains a leading cause of train delays, yet most prediction approaches rely on raw meteorological inputs without exploiting domain-informed feature engineering. This paper investigates machine learning for train delay prediction using the Finland Integrated Train-Weather (FI-TW) dataset, which fuses railway operational records with observations from the Finnish Meteorological Institute's nationwide sensor network of approximately 200 stations communicating over wireless links. We evaluate three feature configurations using XGBoost at Oulu central station (101,146 observations): full weather features, instant weather observations only, and derived weather category scenarios. The category-based approach, employing hierarchical classifications such as Blizzard, Heavy Snow, and Extreme Cold, achieved an R^2 of 0.78, root mean squared error of 8.5 minutes, and mean absolute error of 3.7 minutes, representing an 11% R^2 improvement and 10% error reduction over alternative configurations. These results demonstrate that compact, domain-informed features derived from sensor streams outperform raw meteorological observations, offering bandwidth-efficient representations suitable for edge deployment over current and emerging wireless infrastructures.

AI.tldr: Using domain-informed weather categories from sensor data improves train delay prediction accuracy in Arctic conditions compared to raw meteorological features.
AI.motivation: Reliable railway operations in adverse weather conditions, especially in Arctic regions with extreme temperatures and heavy precipitation, require better prediction methods. Current approaches use raw meteorological inputs without domain-informed feature engineering, leading to suboptimal train delay predictions.
AI.method: The study uses the Finland Integrated Train-Weather (FI-TW) dataset combining railway operational records with weather observations from ~200 Finnish Meteorological Institute stations. Evaluated three XGBoost feature configurations at Oulu central station (101,146 observations): full weather features, instant weather observations only, and derived weather category scenarios using hierarchical classifications like Blizzard, Heavy Snow, and Extreme Cold.
AI.result: The category-based approach achieved R² of 0.78, RMSE of 8.5 minutes, and MAE of 3.7 minutes. This represents an 11% R² improvement and 10% error reduction over alternative configurations using full weather features or instant observations only.
AI.conclusion: Compact, domain-informed features derived from sensor streams outperform raw meteorological observations for train delay prediction. These bandwidth-efficient representations are suitable for edge deployment over current and emerging wireless infrastructures like 6G networks with integrated sensing and computing.

title: Beyond Solver Verdicts: Generative Reward Models for Autoformalization
summary: Neurosymbolic systems rely on mathematical solvers to guarantee reasoning correctness, yet solvers are fundamentally blind to whether a formal translation maintains strict reference-equivalence to a designated formalization. We formalize this vulnerability as Verdict-Preserving-Unfaithfulness (VPU): a failure mode where an incorrect encoding executes successfully and matches the expected verdict. We theoretically prove that structural, verdict-only verification heuristics are mathematically bounded to chance-level detection on these deceptively valid traces. To resolve this, we introduce Generative Verification (GenV), which distills an offline Z3-equivalence oracle into a reference-free, continuous reference-equivalence score by repurposing the language model's native vocabulary space. Mechanistic analysis via decision-projected logit lenses and sparse autoencoders shows this generative readout natively extracts precise spatial error coordinates without explicit localization training. Empirically, our oracle-mined verifier (GenV+HN) achieves 0.961 AUROC in reference-equivalence verification, generalizes zero-shot across unseen translators and divergent formal styles, and yields an 11.3-point downstream accuracy gain in agentic test-time compute allocation.

AI.tldr: Introduces Generative Verification (GenV) to detect Verdict-Preserving-Unfaithfulness in neurosymbolic systems by using language models to score reference-equivalence without explicit references.
AI.motivation: Neurosymbolic systems use mathematical solvers that guarantee reasoning correctness but can't detect when formal translations fail to maintain strict reference-equivalence to the intended formalization, creating a vulnerability called Verdict-Preserving-Unfaithfulness.
AI.method: Introduces Generative Verification (GenV) which distills an offline Z3-equivalence oracle into a reference-free, continuous reference-equivalence score by repurposing language model vocabulary space. Uses mechanistic analysis via decision-projected logit lenses and sparse autoencoders to extract spatial error coordinates.
AI.result: GenV+HN achieves 0.961 AUROC in reference-equivalence verification, generalizes zero-shot across unseen translators and divergent formal styles, and yields 11.3-point downstream accuracy gain in agentic test-time compute allocation.
AI.conclusion: Generative verification provides an effective solution to detect Verdict-Preserving-Unfaithfulness in neurosymbolic systems, enabling reliable reference-equivalence verification without explicit references and improving downstream task performance.

title: Bio-inspired Learning and Decision-Making with Probabilistic In-Memory Computing Hardware: Part 1
summary: Learning and decision-making in animals are often modeled as Bayesian processes, where sensory evidence is integrated with prior beliefs to guide behavior in the face of uncertainty. But what are the inherent neural dynamics that give rise to this ability, and how could they be replicated in computing systems? This abstract discusses a biologically grounded framework in which noisy neural and synaptic dynamics perform inference and learning via stochastic sampling from an internal energy function, capturing uncertainty over latent states and model parameters through neural and synaptic variability, respectively. This enables approaches such as predictive coding networks to account for epistemic uncertainty via Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Drawing a parallel between intrinsic noise in biological systems and electrical noise in emerging probabilistic analogue memory technologies, we highlight how analogue in-memory computing hardware naturally emerges as the solution for massively scalable and energy-efficient probabilistic inference.

AI.tldr: Noisy neural and synaptic dynamics in biological systems perform Bayesian inference through stochastic sampling, which can be replicated in analogue in-memory computing hardware for energy-efficient probabilistic inference at scale.
AI.motivation: Understanding the neural mechanisms behind Bayesian learning in animals and finding ways to replicate these efficient probabilistic inference capabilities in computing systems for scalable, energy-efficient AI.
AI.method: A biologically grounded framework using noisy neural and synaptic dynamics that perform inference and learning via stochastic sampling from an internal energy function, where neural variability captures uncertainty over states and synaptic variability captures uncertainty over parameters.
AI.result: The approach enables predictive coding networks to account for epistemic uncertainty through Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and shows that analogue in-memory computing hardware naturally supports massively scalable and energy-efficient probabilistic inference by leveraging electrical noise similar to biological intrinsic noise.
AI.conclusion: Analogue in-memory computing emerges as the ideal hardware solution for implementing biologically-inspired probabilistic inference at scale, offering energy efficiency and massive parallelism by exploiting the natural noise properties of emerging memory technologies.

title: HERALD: High-Fidelity Exemplar Retrieval with Adaptive Landmark Distillation for Heterophily-Aware Graph Condensation
summary: Graph condensation aims to produce a small surrogate graph that preserves the downstream node-classification performance of a much larger original graph. Existing methods rely on Weisfeiler-Lehman neighbourhood aggregation or gradient-based distribution matching, both of which assume that adjacent nodes share the same label, an assumption that breaks down under heterophily. We propose HERALD (High-fidelity Exemplar Retrieval with Adaptive Landmark Distillation), a gradient-free graph condensation framework that adapts the node scoring and feature selection in the condensation pipeline to the graph's measured heterophily. HERALD selects features via a joint Fisher-discriminability and activation-density criterion that down-weights aggregated representations on heterophilic graphs, and scores nodes by a weighted combination of prototype representativeness, decision-boundary proximity, and Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID), where the weights are driven by a smooth sigmoid function of the heterophily ratio. Nodes are then assembled into a condensed subgraph through score-ordered BFS expansion, Personalised PageRank pruning, and class rebalancing, all at an identical storage budget to BONSAI, enabling direct comparison. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets spanning homophilic and heterophilic settings show that HERALD matches or outperforms state-of-the-art condensers on heterophilic graphs and remains competitive on homophilic ones across four GNN architectures.

AI.tldr: HERALD is a gradient-free graph condensation framework that adapts to graph heterophily, outperforming existing methods on heterophilic graphs while remaining competitive on homophilic ones.
AI.motivation: Existing graph condensation methods rely on assumptions that adjacent nodes share the same label, which breaks down under heterophily (nodes connecting to dissimilar nodes). Current methods using Weisfeiler-Lehman aggregation or gradient-based distribution matching don't handle heterophilic graphs well.
AI.method: HERALD uses a gradient-free approach with: 1) Feature selection via joint Fisher-discriminability and activation-density that down-weights aggregated representations on heterophilic graphs, 2) Node scoring combining prototype representativeness, decision-boundary proximity, and Local Intrinsic Dimensionality weighted by a sigmoid function of heterophily ratio, 3) Condensed subgraph assembly through score-ordered BFS expansion, Personalised PageRank pruning, and class rebalancing at identical storage budget to BONSAI.
AI.result: Experiments on eight benchmark datasets spanning homophilic and heterophilic settings show HERALD matches or outperforms state-of-the-art condensers on heterophilic graphs and remains competitive on homophilic ones across four GNN architectures.
AI.conclusion: HERALD successfully addresses the limitation of existing graph condensation methods in heterophilic settings through adaptive, gradient-free techniques, demonstrating robust performance across diverse graph types while maintaining storage efficiency.

title: When Does Text Inform? Benchmarking Information-Theoretic Metrics for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal forecasting models that combine time series with text annotations promise richer prediction through textual context, but how do we know whether a text annotation meaningfully contributes to the forecasters prediction? This is an information-theoretic question, but to evaluate whether information-theoretic metrics can reliably measure the predictive value an annotation provides, a ground truth benchmark is needed, and none currently exist. We create a synthetic time series signal with annotations in three categories: semantically correct, incorrect, and irrelevant. Because the data generation process is fully controlled, ground-truth information content is known exactly, enabling principled evaluation of six complementary mutual information estimators (KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID and V-information). We show that all six estimators identify correct annotations as most informative, and are able to audit the quality of mixed text corpora, choosing the annotations that result in the best downstream forecasting results without the need for model training. Our benchmark identifies limitations of each estimator, and these are validated on seven real-world datasets, which show how estimator performance differs on weak signals. Finally, we establish practical rules for implementing these metrics for annotation auditing and fusion selection.

AI.tldr: A benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic metrics that measure whether text annotations meaningfully contribute to time series forecasting, with validation on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Need to determine whether text annotations meaningfully contribute to multimodal forecasting models, requiring evaluation of information-theoretic metrics that currently lack ground truth benchmarks.
AI.method: Created synthetic time series with controlled text annotations in three categories (correct, incorrect, irrelevant), enabling exact ground-truth information measurement. Evaluated six mutual information estimators (KSG, MINE, InfoNCE, CCA, PID, V-information).
AI.result: All six estimators correctly identified informative annotations and could audit text corpora quality without model training. Benchmark revealed limitations of each estimator, validated on seven real-world datasets showing performance differences on weak signals.
AI.conclusion: Established practical rules for implementing information-theoretic metrics for annotation auditing and fusion selection in multimodal forecasting models.

title: How Wrong Can a Good Predictor Be? Diverging Updates with Vanishing Predictive KL
summary: Accurate posterior prediction need not require accurate approximation of Bayesian updates. We prove that an unbounded gap between the update maps can coexist with vanishing predictive KL for every fixed finite $K\ge2$ in a stationary symmetric Gaussian HMM. Exact Bayesian mixing and an explicit deterministic radial filter act on the same $K-1$ belief coordinates. As $q\to0^+$, their separation in centered logits in the worst case grows at least linearly in the natural confidence scale $L_K(q)$, while their categorical $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathrm{exact}\|\mathrm{radial})$ vanishes at the same explicit witness. Along stationary HMM trajectories, the expected terminal KL between filtered posteriors also converges to zero at $H(q)=\lceil-\log(q)/c\rceil+1$. Typical blocks without switches drive both filters into a common confidence cone, where softmax curvature suppresses their disagreement; a single Gaussian maximal event controls adaptive noise. A sweep with equally spaced Gaussians over $K\in\{2,4,8\}$ illustrates the opposing trends, and binary controls at long horizons compare saturating and nonsaturating recurrences. The result isolates two missing links between internal update gaps and predictive cost: the contribution of separating states to expected loss and decoder sensitivity. Thus even an unbounded internal update gap does not by itself certify predictive failure. The construction is fixed in $K$ and does not provide a universal criterion for when compression is harmless or characterize when internal gaps must incur task loss.

AI.tldr: Even when Bayesian approximation has unbounded internal update errors, predictive performance can still be perfect in certain Gaussian HMM settings.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the conventional assumption that accurate posterior prediction requires accurate Bayesian updates. It investigates whether predictive performance can remain good even when update approximations have large internal errors.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using stationary symmetric Gaussian Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). Compares exact Bayesian mixing with an explicit deterministic radial filter. Studies the gap between their update maps while examining predictive KL divergence vanishing to zero. Uses mathematical analysis with parameters like switching probability q, confidence scales, and categorical KL divergence metrics.
AI.result: Proves that unbounded gap between update maps can coexist with vanishing predictive KL for every fixed finite K≥2. Shows that as switching probability q→0⁺, update separation grows linearly in confidence scale while categorical KL vanishes. Demonstrates expected terminal KL between filtered posteriors converges to zero. Identifies mechanisms where typical blocks without switches drive both filters into common confidence cone where softmax curvature suppresses disagreement.
AI.conclusion: Even an unbounded internal update gap does not necessarily certify predictive failure. The paper isolates missing links between internal update gaps and predictive cost: contribution of separating states to expected loss and decoder sensitivity. However, the analysis is limited to fixed K and doesn't provide universal criteria for when compression is harmless or when internal gaps must incur task loss.

title: Generating a Consistent Enterprise: Synthesis and Reference-Free Evaluation of Multi-System Business Data
summary: Synthetic relational data is normally produced by a model trained on a real dataset, and its quality is measured as the distance to that dataset. This paper describes a generator that has no real dataset at either end. Given an industry, a company size, a business model, a set of business applications, and a random seed, it produces a complete fictional enterprise: a workforce, a customer base, sales deals, support tickets, recorded calls, chat messages, and documents, all consistent with one another. One entity graph is projected into the native formats of 66 business products, so the same customer appears in the CRM, the support desk, and the call system under one identity. Because no real counterpart exists, realism is built in from cited reference statistics and verified by reference-free measurement: a five-axis scorecard of 28 statistical checks, an adversarial detector that hunts for the marks of synthetic generation, and a set of soundness checks that include a classifier test against an independently shuffled copy of the data. Because these instruments existed before the generator was tuned, progress is measured under a fixed yardstick: over 23 generated companies, mean realism climbed from 60.3 to 99.1, the weakest company from 41.1 to 94.9, and the detector, which initially flagged 55.2% of all records, now flags none. The scores hold on a seed never used during development. A second generator builds relational databases from a list of business questions. It forces qualifying rows for each answerable question, adds controlled near misses, and computes exact labels from the finished tables. The generator runs as a hosted service at https://console.era.eon.io. A company built there to a specification is served through its simulators over MCP and REST, and the simulators are also published as container images for offline use

AI.tldr: A generator creates complete fictional enterprise data without real-world training data, projecting entities into 66 business formats with statistical realism verified by reference-free metrics.
AI.motivation: Traditional synthetic data generation relies on real datasets and measures quality by distance to that dataset, but this approach can't create data for non-existent scenarios or may inherit biases from real data.
AI.method: 1. Creates fictional enterprises using industry, company size, business model, applications, and random seed. 2. Projects entity graphs into 66 native business formats. 3. Builds realism from cited reference statistics. 4. Uses reference-free verification: five-axis scorecard (28 checks), adversarial detector, and classifier tests. 5. Second generator creates relational databases from business questions with forced qualifying rows and near misses.
AI.result: Mean realism improved from 60.3 to 99.1 across 23 companies, weakest company from 41.1 to 94.9. Adversarial detector initially flagged 55.2% of records, now flags none. Results hold on unseen seeds. System available as hosted service at https://console.era.eon.io.
AI.conclusion: This approach enables high-quality synthetic enterprise data generation without real-world training data, with rigorous statistical verification. The system provides practical utility through hosted services and offline containers for realistic business data simulation.

title: Phase-Decoupled, Model-Calibrated Power Control for Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary: Datacenter GPU power is the binding constraint on LLM serving capacity, and production serving has shifted to prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation. Deploying NVIDIA's Max-Q inference profile on a disaggregated B200 system, we found its realized gain modest (+8.6% tokens/J), model-dependent, and carrying a mean end-to-end latency cost (+5.2%) that throughput-only evaluation does not surface; the profile also applies one setting to prefill and decode GPUs that operate in opposite hardware regimes. We hypothesize that the optimal power setting is a property of the deployed (model, quantization, engine, hardware) combination rather than of the GPU class, that each lane warrants its own profile, and that converting SLO headroom into energy safely requires latency-gated calibration under a runtime SLO guard rather than a fixed recipe.
