AI.conclusion: Calibration gives confidence thresholds explicit selective-risk interpretation, creating unified decision criteria that decouple deployment policies from specific model pools or operating budgets, enabling more flexible and reliable heterogeneous model collaboration.

title: Estimating Inconsistency Response Surfaces under Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical System Development
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IEEE ICDM 2026; 10 pages + appendix, 11 figures, 3 tables
summary: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are commonly represented through multiple interconnected models. During development, CPS consistency requires that shared model elements remain compatible across these models. Uncertainty, for example, due to sensor noise or model abstraction, changes the admissible values of model elements and can introduce inconsistencies, i.e., situations in which models can no longer be jointly satisfied. While existing approaches can determine consistency for a given uncertainty configuration, they provide limited support for systematically exploring, analyzing, and explaining inconsistency across large uncertainty spaces. We address this challenge by reformulating inconsistency as an intervention response modeling problem. Using Saltelli sampling and multi-fidelity Monte Carlo estimation, we generate intervention-response datasets and train a surrogate model that directly predicts inconsistency from the propagated uncertainty geometry. Experiments on 48 scenarios and 10 CPS domains show that the surrogate matches Monte Carlo estimates while reducing evaluation time from milliseconds to microseconds, enabling orders-of-magnitude more response-surface evaluations within fixed computational budgets. Building on the learned response surfaces, we perform sensitivity analysis to identify dominant uncertainty drivers and introduce a gradient-based consistency recourse method to determine minimal uncertainty interventions that restore consistency. The results show that inconsistency under uncertainty can be effectively learned, analyzed, and repaired through response-surface modeling, providing a scalable foundation for uncertainty-aware consistency management in CPS development.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a response-surface modeling approach using surrogate models and sensitivity analysis to efficiently detect, analyze, and repair inconsistency problems in Cyber-Physical Systems under uncertainty, achieving orders-of-magnitude speed improvements over Monte Carlo methods.
AI.motivation: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) use interconnected models where shared elements must remain compatible. Uncertainty from sources like sensor noise or model abstraction can change admissible values and introduce inconsistencies that prevent models from being jointly satisfied. Existing approaches only determine consistency for specific uncertainty configurations but lack systematic methods for exploring, analyzing, and explaining inconsistency across large uncertainty spaces.
AI.method: Reformulates inconsistency as an intervention-response modeling problem. Uses Saltelli sampling and multi-fidelity Monte Carlo estimation to generate intervention-response datasets. Trains a surrogate model that directly predicts inconsistency from propagated uncertainty geometry. Performs sensitivity analysis on learned response surfaces to identify dominant uncertainty drivers, and introduces a gradient-based consistency recourse method to determine minimal uncertainty interventions that restore consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on 48 scenarios across 10 CPS domains show the surrogate model matches Monte Carlo estimates while reducing evaluation time from milliseconds to microseconds, enabling orders-of-magnitude more response-surface evaluations within fixed computational budgets. The approach effectively learns, analyzes, and repairs inconsistency through response-surface modeling.
AI.conclusion: Inconsistency under uncertainty in CPS can be effectively learned, analyzed, and repaired through response-surface modeling, providing a scalable foundation for uncertainty-aware consistency management in CPS development.

title: RouteRepair: Instance-Level Failure Diagnosis and Targeted Repair in LLM-Based Automated Heuristic Design for Routing Optimization
summary: Efficient routing optimization is essential to freight transportation, urban logistics, and shared mobility, where high-quality heuristics are often required under limited computational budgets. Recent large language model (LLM)-based automated heuristic design methods can generate effective routing rules, but aggregate evaluation may mask recurrent failures on particular instance structures. To address this limitation, this study develops RouteRepair, which diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from instance-level performance and applies targeted modifications to the corresponding heuristic components while protecting behavior that already performs well. Routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context are combined to define bounded repair objectives, and each intervention is validated through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation. Experiments on the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) span constructive search, guided local search, and ant colony optimization. RouteRepair-GLS reduces the mean TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, while the constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic; the generated ACO priors also outperform matched hand-designed priors. These results show that failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well.

AI.tldr: RouteRepair is an LLM-based method that diagnoses specific weaknesses in routing heuristics and applies targeted repairs to improve performance on difficult instances while preserving existing good behavior.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based automated heuristic design methods for routing problems suffer from a limitation: they evaluate performance in aggregate, which can mask recurrent failures on specific instance structures. This means heuristics may perform well on average but fail consistently on certain types of problems.
AI.method: RouteRepair analyzes parent-specific weaknesses through instance-level performance diagnosis, then applies targeted modifications to problematic heuristic components while protecting well-performing behaviors. It combines routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context to define bounded repair objectives, and validates each intervention through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation.
AI.result: RouteRepair significantly improves routing heuristics on TSP and CVRP across multiple algorithms: RouteRepair-GLS reduces TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, the constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% compared to savings heuristic, and generated ACO priors outperform hand-designed priors.
AI.conclusion: Failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can effectively improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well, demonstrating the value of targeted, instance-specific repairs over aggregate evaluations.

title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Knowledge graph foundation models can be simplified by reifying graphs into a fixed meta-relational structure, enabling standard GNNs to achieve zero-shot transfer across multiple benchmarks without dedicated architectures.
AI.motivation: Current knowledge graph foundation models like ULTRA use dedicated architectures with hard-coded transfer mechanisms for zero-shot link prediction. The authors aim to move this transfer capability from the architecture into the representation itself, simplifying the approach and making it more generalizable.
AI.method: The paper proposes reifying knowledge graphs by converting each fact into a node, connecting it to its subject, object, and relation type through six fixed meta-relations. Relation types become anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. This representation allows standard GNNs (GAT, GINE, GraphSAGE, R-GCN) to be trained on a single small graph and transfer zero-shot to various benchmarks.
AI.result: Five standard GNNs trained on just 4,245 triples for 30 minutes achieved zero-shot transfer to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. A GAT model matched the performance of ULTRA, which requires dedicated pre-training on multiple graphs. The approach also extends to relational databases, showing strong performance on foreign-key prediction tasks without schema or cell values.
AI.conclusion: The transfer mechanism for knowledge graph reasoning can be embedded in the graph representation rather than requiring specialized architectures. Standard GNNs with reified graph representations can achieve foundation-model-level performance with minimal training, offering a simpler and more generalizable approach to zero-shot link prediction across diverse domains.

title: Flexible and Interpretable Accent Distance Measurements
summary: Determining the differences between two speakers' accents is a fundamental task in linguistics and speech technology research. The methodology used to measure these differences depends on the specific research area. A phonetics researcher may demonstrate accent variation by comparing vowel formants in paired recordings of individual words. These results will be interpretable, but the recordings will be time-consuming to collect and may not be representative of connected speech. Accented Text-to-Speech (TTS) research has pushed towards using accent embeddings derived from accent classification tasks. These embeddings can be produced from any speech recording, but are not readily interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate that articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion can be used as an interpretable basis for accent comparison and that optimal transport provides a framework for accent comparison across arbitrary recording types.

AI.tldr: Using articulatory inversion and optimal transport for interpretable accent comparison across different speech recordings
AI.motivation: Current methods for comparing speaker accents have limitations: phonetics approaches (using vowel formants) are time-consuming and may not represent connected speech, while TTS accent embeddings are not interpretable despite being producible from any recording.
AI.method: The paper proposes using articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion as an interpretable basis for accent comparison, combined with optimal transport to enable comparison across arbitrary recording types.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate that their approach works as an interpretable method for accent comparison that can handle different types of recordings, bridging the gap between interpretable but limited phonetics methods and flexible but opaque TTS embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Articulatory representations with optimal transport provide a viable framework for interpretable accent comparison that overcomes the limitations of existing methods by being both interpretable and applicable to various recording types.

title: Local Robustness Quantification for Naive Bayes Classifiers and Generative Forests: a General Approach
summary: We provide methods for calculating the robustness of the predictions of two types of generative classifiers whose underlying distribution is a Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM): naive Bayes classifiers and generative forests (a probabilistic extension of random forests). Following the paradigm of robustness quantification, we define the robustness of a prediction as the extent to which the distribution of the classifier can be perturbed without changing this prediction. We consider perturbations obtained by varying the local models of the PGMs within general neighborhoods and focus in particular on epsilon-contamination, total variation distance and chi-squared divergence balls. We test our methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrate that the robustness value of a prediction serves as an indicator for its trustworthiness and compare our approach with other such indicators.

AI.tldr: Methods for calculating prediction robustness in generative classifiers based on Probabilistic Graphical Models (naive Bayes and generative forests) by measuring how much the underlying distribution can be perturbed without changing predictions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide quantitative methods for assessing the trustworthiness of predictions made by generative classifiers, particularly when these classifiers are based on Probabilistic Graphical Models. The paper aims to define and measure prediction robustness to help identify reliable predictions.
AI.method: The authors define prediction robustness as the extent to which the classifier's distribution can be perturbed without changing the prediction. They consider perturbations by varying the local models of PGMs within neighborhoods defined by epsilon-contamination, total variation distance, and chi-squared divergence balls. The methods are applied to naive Bayes classifiers and generative forests.
AI.result: The methods were tested on benchmark datasets, demonstrating that the robustness value of a prediction serves as an effective indicator for its trustworthiness. The approach was compared with other trustworthiness indicators to validate its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robustness quantification framework provides a valuable tool for assessing prediction trustworthiness in generative classifiers based on Probabilistic Graphical Models, offering practical methods for identifying reliable predictions in applications of naive Bayes and generative forest classifiers.

title: The Convention Gap: Towards Measuring Implicit Communication in Cooperative AI Evaluation
summary: Cooperative AI agents are evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation relies on implicit conventions---shared protocols for reading meaning beyond the literal message---which AI-AI benchmarks may not capture. We propose the \emph{convention gap}, the difference between the failure probability predicted from the literal content of communication and the observed failure rate, as a metric of implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, the finite deck and deterministic hint constraints make this posterior exactly computable. We replayed about 101,000 play actions from three public datasets of human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData) games. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in human pairs, $-$0.7~pp in AI pairs, and +16.4~pp in human-AI pairs, and was concentrated on plays of cards that had received no hints (+46~pp in human pairs). Within human-AI play, the literal information available to humans was similar across the three AI partners (mean predicted failure 38--41\%), but human failure rates ranged from 14.4\% to 34.4\% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2~pp; the partner eliciting the largest gap produced the fewest human failures. Game score carried different information: it depended on each corpus's roster composition, whereas the gap separated human from AI play at the agent level. As a known-answer check, Off-Belief Learning agents, whose convention content is controlled by construction, gave a gap of +1.6~pp at the convention-free level, rising monotonically to +21.7~pp. These results suggest that convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "convention gap" metric to measure implicit communication in cooperative AI, showing that human pairs have a +26.2pp gap while AI pairs have almost none, suggesting AI-AI benchmarks don't capture human-like cooperative communication.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents are evaluated against other AIs, but human cooperation relies on implicit conventions and shared protocols that go beyond literal communication. Existing AI-AI benchmarks may not capture these important aspects of human collaboration.
AI.method: The authors propose the "convention gap" - the difference between predicted failure probability from literal communication content and observed failure rate. They analyze Hanabi gameplay data from three datasets: human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData), totaling about 101,000 play actions. They also test Off-Belief Learning agents as a known-answer check.
AI.result: Human pairs showed a +26.2pp convention gap, AI pairs showed -0.7pp, and human-AI pairs showed +16.4pp. The gap was concentrated on plays of cards that received no hints (+46pp in human pairs). Among human-AI play, different AI partners elicited different gaps (from +24.1 to +6.2pp) despite similar literal information available. Game score depended on corpus composition, while the gap separated human from AI play at the agent level. Off-Belief Learning agents showed a controllable gap from +1.6pp to +21.7pp.
AI.conclusion: Convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may better predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners. The convention gap metric successfully captures implicit communication patterns in human cooperation that are largely absent in AI-AI interactions.

title: Prevalence Determines Precision:Silent Contamination in Detector-Defined Datasets
summary: Many ML datasets are constructed by running a detector, heuristic, or model over candidate pools; accepted items become labels. Dataset precision is then governed by true-positive prevalence in each pool via Bayes, not solely by detector quality. Using one instrument and period, we hold a detector-defined event dataset plus an independent official index labeling every detected item as real or phantom. One detector, three pools yield phantom rates 81.7%, 9.0%, and 0.0%. Transferring precision from the two high-rate pools to the low-rate pool predicts 0.955 versus measured 0.183, a +422% error; the Bayes expression predicts all three within 3.3%. The detected response curve is an exact convex combination of a true-event and a phantom component (residual 1.1e-16), with phantoms outnumbering true events 473 to 308, so contamination is a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise. Contamination direction depends on the estimator: on identical windows one statistic is diluted and another inflated because its denominator is also contaminated. A common normalization turns the estimator into a mean of ratios whose expectation need not exist; on the same 335 events it returns 0.40 where the well-defined estimator returns 0.10.

AI.tldr: ML dataset precision depends on true-positive prevalence in candidate pools via Bayes' theorem, not just detector quality. Analysis shows phantom events (false positives) outnumber true events, and contamination behaves as a second signal with detector-inherited shape rather than additive noise.
AI.motivation: Many machine learning datasets are constructed by applying detectors/heuristics over candidate pools, where accepted items become labels. The precision of such datasets is commonly misunderstood - it's governed by true-positive prevalence in each pool via Bayes' theorem, not solely by detector quality.
AI.method: Using a detector-defined event dataset with an independent official index labeling every detected item as real or phantom, the study analyzes three different pools. It applies Bayes' theorem to predict precision, decomposes the detected response curve into true-event and phantom components, and examines how different estimators behave on contaminated data.
AI.result: Three pools showed phantom rates of 81.7%, 9.0%, and 0.0%. Transferring precision from high-rate pools to low-rate pool yielded +422% error, while Bayes' theorem predicted all three within 3.3%. The response curve decomposes exactly into true-event and phantom components (residual 1.1e-16), with phantoms outnumbering true events 473:308. Different estimators show opposite effects: one statistic diluted, another inflated due to denominator contamination.
AI.conclusion: Dataset contamination from detectors behaves as a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise. The direction of contamination effect depends on the estimator used - some are diluted while others are inflated. A common normalization method can produce unreliable results (0.40 vs 0.10 on same events), highlighting the importance of proper statistical formulation in dataset construction.

title: Published Unlearning Numbers Move Per Checkpoint, and Not Because the Removed Data Survives: An Audit of 263 Released Batch-Normalized Checkpoints
comment: 38 pages, 4 figures, 26 tables. Independent of and concurrent with arXiv:2609.08901 (posted 8 Sep 2026): the instrument and protocol here were pre-registered on 29 Aug 2026; dated provenance in Appendix S
summary: An unlearning audit reads its verdict off numbers that an unlearned model and its retrained reference each publish, and both also ship batch-normalization statistics that no gradient step wrote and no release records. Refitting them on kept data at bit-identical weights moves 47 of 221 released checkpoints past the spread their own release's seeds show, several inside a method whose average does not move: what moves is the checkpoint's property, not its method's. What does the moving is not the removed data surviving in the state: exchanging kept records for removed ones inside a fixed fitting pool moves a published cell by almost nothing, while how far a checkpoint's shipped state has drifted from any refit does track it. The consequence for a published decision is real but narrow: twelve verdicts cross, four clear a measured recalibration budget, two clear it on every replicate, and a population we trained and sited near its own criterion yields none. A release should therefore name the fitting convention beside the number, on the batch-normalized vision models where this channel exists.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates vulnerabilities in machine unlearning audits when models use batch normalization statistics that weren't properly tracked during training, showing that refitting these statistics can change audit outcomes for 47 of 221 checkpoints.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the observation that unlearning audits rely on numerical comparisons between unlearned models and retrained references, but these comparisons can be compromised when models use batch normalization statistics that aren't properly recorded or tracked during the training/unlearning process. These statistics are "shipped" with released checkpoints but aren't documented in release records.
AI.method: The researchers refit batch normalization statistics on kept data at bit-identical weights for released checkpoints. They examine how this affects audit outcomes, test whether removed data persists in model states by exchanging kept and removed records, and track how far checkpoints' shipped states have drifted from refits. They also train populations near decision criteria to test robustness.
AI.result: Refitting batch normalization statistics moved 47 of 221 released checkpoints beyond the spread shown by release seeds, with several moving within a method whose average doesn't change (showing checkpoint-specific effects). The movement isn't due to residual removed data, as exchanging kept/removed records has minimal effect. Twelve audit verdicts changed, four cleared a recalibration budget, two cleared it on every replicate, but populations trained near decision criteria showed no crossing.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that batch normalization statistics pose a real but narrow vulnerability for unlearning audits in vision models. Releases should document the fitting convention alongside numerical results to ensure audit validity, particularly for batch-normalized vision models where this channel exists.

title: Combining Synthetic and Real Data for Low-Resource Historical OCR: A Manchu Case Study
summary: Manchu, now critically endangered, was one of the principal languages of the Qing empire (1636-1912), and its extensive archival record is increasingly digitized but remains difficult to search and analyze at scale. Previous work showed that vision-language models (VLMs) trained only on synthetic Manchu word images can reach 87.4% word accuracy on real Qing manuscripts and prints, leaving a substantial synthetic-to-real gap. This study examines how synthetic and real historical training data should be combined for low-resource OCR. Using 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images, we evaluate three pretrained VLMs and a compact convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) under four regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training, following a common checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Introducing real training images raises the leading configurations to between 95.09% and 96.28% word accuracy, while no synthetic-only configuration exceeds 87.92%. Synthetic supplementation substantially improves all three VLMs, whereas its marginal effect for the CRNN is sensitive to the training objective. Joint and sequential training yield broadly similar archival accuracy under the tested practical pipelines. A compact CRNN also reaches the leading performance range once real images are available, showing that model scale alone does not determine recognition accuracy. Finally, complementary errors among strong recognizers allow voting to raise accuracy to 98.27% without additional training, while an eighteenth-century Manchu dictionary provides a principled rule for adjudicating disagreements.

AI.tldr: Combining synthetic and real historical training data significantly improves Manchu OCR accuracy, with best configurations achieving 95-96% word accuracy, and ensemble voting reaching 98.27% without additional training.
AI.motivation: Manchu is critically endangered but has extensive digitized archives that are difficult to search and analyze at scale. Previous OCR methods using only synthetic training data showed a substantial synthetic-to-real gap (87.4% accuracy), leaving room for improvement in historical document recognition.
AI.method: Used 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images to evaluate three pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and a compact CRNN under four training regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training. Also implemented ensemble voting and used an 18th-century Manchu dictionary for rule-based adjudication of disagreements.
AI.result: Introducing real training images raised accuracy to 95.09-96.28% word accuracy (vs max 87.92% synthetic-only). Synthetic supplementation substantially improved all three VLMs. Joint and sequential training yielded similar accuracy. A compact CRNN also reached leading performance once real images were available. Ensemble voting raised accuracy to 98.27% without additional training.
AI.conclusion: For low-resource OCR of historical scripts like Manchu, combining synthetic and real training data is crucial for high accuracy. Model scale alone doesn't determine performance when sufficient real data is available. Ensemble methods and historical dictionaries can further boost accuracy, making historical document analysis more accessible.

title: DeFiFlowBench: Benchmarking and Improving Safe Executability in Natural-Language DeFi Workflow Synthesis
summary: A structurally valid DeFi workflow can still authorize a costly trade. We introduce DeFiFlowBench, a benchmark of 207 team-authored prompts for natural-language DeFi workflow synthesis. It measures graph coverage, configuration completeness, and declared safety predicates, then tests supported trade configurations on a local EVM. Direct, constrained, and few-shot prompting produce 14-19 unsafe held-out executions per configuration under a fixed 5% price-impact cap. A slippage bound derived from a quote does not prevent the price impact of the order itself. We propose Koan-Safe, which combines a prompt-only intent parser, a replaceable generator, and structural repair with default safety parameters. On 75 held-out workflow prompts, its hybrid variant scores 0.67 on the static safety proxy, compared with 0.33 for the best baseline. Koan-Safe records no unsafe executions on the saved benchmark outputs. A matched-candidate ablation produces 14-17 unsafe executions when enforcement is disabled. Additional tests expose the limits of default injection: permissive existing thresholds can still authorize unsafe trades. A separately evaluated policy cap addresses this failure on a 36-case diagnostic grid. These results support explicit trade protections and execution-based evaluation, while distinguishing declared safety from a general guarantee.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (DeFiFlowBench) for DeFi workflow synthesis reveals safety issues, and a proposed system (Koan-Safe) with structural repair improves safety but still faces limits with default protections.
AI.motivation: Structurally valid DeFi workflows can still authorize costly trades due to safety issues. Current approaches don't adequately prevent unsafe executions despite declared safety measures.
AI.method: Created DeFiFlowBench benchmark with 207 prompts for DeFi workflow synthesis, measuring graph coverage, configuration completeness, and safety predicates. Tested multiple prompting strategies (direct, constrained, few-shot) and proposed Koan-Safe system with intent parser, replaceable generator, and structural repair with default safety parameters.
AI.result: Baseline prompting produces 14-19 unsafe executions per configuration. Koan-Safe's hybrid variant scores 0.67 on static safety proxy vs 0.33 for best baseline, with no unsafe executions on saved benchmark outputs. However, default injection has limits as permissive thresholds can still authorize unsafe trades.
AI.conclusion: Explicit trade protections and execution-based evaluation are needed. Declared safety doesn't guarantee general safety, and a separately evaluated policy cap can address remaining failures in DeFi workflow synthesis.

title: ActMap: Single-Pass Uncertainty Quantification from Generation-Time Activation Maps
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Includes technical appendix
summary:
Practical uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models must decide,
  from a single generation, whether a specific answer should be trusted. Existing
  methods either sample multiple generations, read only output-token probabilities,
  or reduce the model's internal computation to a single hidden state. We introduce
  ActMap, a white-box representation that compresses the generation-time hidden-
  state trajectory (every layer, every generated token) into a fixed $12 \times 32
  \times 128$ tensor of temporal-statistic channels that preserves structure across
  transformer depth and pooled hidden coordinates. The map is captured during the
  generation pass with no measurable overhead, has a fixed shape across model
  depths and hidden sizes, and occupies 96 KiB: a compact artifact that can be
  retained for audit-relevant generations and probed directly, with occlusion
  analysis localizing the classifier's signal to mid-depth regions of the map. A
  lightweight classifier, instantiated as a compact Vision Transformer, reads an
  estimated correctness probability from each map in a fraction of a millisecond;
  capacity-matched MLPs perform comparably, indicating the representation itself
  carries the result. Trained and evaluated in-domain on short-answer QA, direct-
  answer math, and summarization factuality with three instruction-tuned 7-8B
  models, ActMap consistently outperforms sampling, token-probability, attention,
  and embedding baselines, and matches ACT-ViT, a detector trained on dense
  activation tensors $67 \times$ larger, at essentially the same mean AUROC with
  lower calibration error on ten of twelve pairs. The resulting score supports
  abstention, routing, and selective verification from a single generation, making
  it a practical primitive for scalable oversight of deployed models.

AI.tldr: ActMap: A compact 96 KiB white-box representation capturing transformer activation trajectories for uncertainty quantification from single generations, outperforming baselines while matching much larger detectors.
AI.motivation: Current uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs have limitations: they either require multiple generations (sampling), only use output-token probabilities, or reduce internal computations to single hidden states. There's a need for a practical UQ method that works from single generations while leveraging rich internal model information.
AI.method: ActMap compresses the generation-time hidden-state trajectory (every layer, every generated token) into a fixed 12×32×128 tensor of temporal-statistic channels. It captures structure across transformer depth and pooled hidden coordinates during generation with no measurable overhead. A lightweight classifier (compact Vision Transformer) reads correctness probabilities from each map in <1ms.
AI.result: ActMap consistently outperforms sampling, token-probability, attention, and embedding baselines on short-answer QA, math, and summarization tasks with 7-8B models. It matches ACT-ViT (67× larger activation tensors) at essentially same mean AUROC with lower calibration error on 10/12 pairs.
AI.conclusion: ActMap provides a practical uncertainty quantification primitive for scalable oversight, supporting abstention, routing, and selective verification from single generations with minimal overhead and compact storage.

title: Generalized Score Matching for Parameter Estimation on Convex Domains
summary: Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation is a principled and statistically efficient approach for learning probabilistic models. However, for unnormalized models, ML estimation requires evaluating the partition function and differentiating through it, which may not always be tractable. Score matching provides a practically viable alternative that circumvents this obstacle by fitting the score in a way that eliminates dependence on the normalizing constant. We derive the generalized score matching objective on a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ constructively starting from Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning, and show how classical score matching as well as domain-adapted variants for non-negative data arise naturally within the proposed framework. We show that the resulting objective is a {\it proper local scoring rule} of second-order, which provides the theoretical guarantee that the true density is recovered when the objective is minimized. Furthermore, for a model belonging to the exponential family, we establish convexity of the objective together with consistency of the finite-sample estimator under standard regularity conditions. Our derivation sheds new light on the scope and applicability of generalized score matching in various problem settings. We compare generalized score matching-based estimators on constrained domains, where the partition function is analytically intractable. We provide experimental results on parameter estimation for model densities belonging to the exponential family defined over convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and a generative modeling use-case to demonstrate broader applicability of the proposed generalized score matching framework.

AI.tldr: Generalized score matching is derived as a tractable alternative to ML estimation for unnormalized models on constrained domains, providing theoretical guarantees and practical applications.
AI.motivation: Maximum likelihood estimation for unnormalized models requires evaluating the partition function, which can be computationally intractable, especially for models on constrained domains like convex subsets of ℝ^d.
AI.method: Derives generalized score matching objective from Minimum Probability Flow learning, showing how classical score matching and domain-adapted variants emerge naturally. Demonstrates it's a proper local scoring rule of second-order and establishes convexity for exponential family models.
AI.result: Generalized score matching eliminates partition function dependence, recovers true density when minimized, and for exponential family models, yields convex objectives with consistent estimators under standard conditions.
AI.conclusion: Generalized score matching provides a theoretically sound and practical framework for learning unnormalized models on constrained domains, with broader applicability beyond parameter estimation to generative modeling tasks.

title: Extending SMT Solving with Non-Ground Clause Learning
summary: Quantifier instantiation is currently the main approach to non-ground SMT solving: solvers generate ground instances and solve the resulting ground SMT problems with CDCL(T)-style reasoning. When a conflict is found, conflict analysis learns only a ground clause, even though the conflict comes from instances of non-ground clauses. Yet non-ground reasoning can give exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. We propose a calculus that consists of ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style rules, and non-ground conflict analysis. The solver reasons on ground instances, but the resolution steps of conflict analysis are performed on their original non-ground clauses. This produces learned clauses that are typically more general than the ground conflict. With a suitable strategy, the learned clauses are even non-redundant. We also show how chronological backtracking can be included in SMT solving. Our calculus gives a common setting for CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, a range of instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, and we prove that it simulates CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution.

AI.tldr: A new SMT calculus combines ground instantiation, CDCL(T)-style reasoning, and non-ground conflict analysis to produce more general learned clauses, potentially enabling exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current quantifier instantiation approaches in SMT solving only learn ground clauses from conflicts, even when conflicts originate from non-ground clauses. Since non-ground reasoning can provide exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning, there's a need to incorporate non-ground conflict analysis into SMT solving frameworks.
AI.method: The proposed calculus combines three components: ground instantiations (generating ground instances), CDCL(T)-style reasoning (solving resulting ground SMT problems), and non-ground conflict analysis (performing resolution steps on original non-ground clauses instead of their ground instances). The solver reasons on ground instances but learns clauses that are more general than ground conflicts.
AI.result: The approach produces learned clauses that are typically more general than ground conflicts, and with suitable strategy, can be non-redundant. The calculus also shows how chronological backtracking can be included in SMT solving. The framework provides a common setting that simulates various existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed calculus unifies CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, proving that it can simulate CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution, offering a more powerful framework for SMT solving with quantifiers.

title: Particle GFlowNets: Rethinking Generative Marginalization Models
summary: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) have been recently introduced as efficient neural sampling models for any-order autoregressive modelling of discrete distributions. By learning both the marginal and conditional probabilities of a persistent-block Gibbs sampler, MaMs enable fast posterior evaluation with a single neural network forward pass. While prior work has considered MaMs to be distinct from Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), a well-established paradigm for inference in discrete stochastic models, we show that they are equivalent. Then, we also extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes. In particular, we describe an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler, derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic, which plays a key role in speeding up learning convergence. Our experiments show that our method, called Particle GFlowNets, markedly accelerates training in large combinatorial spaces.

AI.tldr: Particle GFlowNets unify Generative Marginalization Models and GFlowNets, extending them with non-autoregressive processes and automatic rejuvenation criteria to accelerate training in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to bridge two seemingly distinct paradigms - Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) - for efficient discrete distribution modeling, and to address training convergence issues in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.method: The authors establish equivalence between MaMs and GFlowNets, then extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive processes. They introduce automatic full-state rejuvenation using a criterion derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic for the Gibbs sampler.
AI.result: The proposed method, Particle GFlowNets, shows marked acceleration of training convergence in large combinatorial spaces compared to previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: MaMs and GFlowNets are fundamentally equivalent, and their unified framework with automatic rejuvenation (Particle GFlowNets) significantly improves training efficiency for discrete stochastic models in combinatorial spaces.

title: Lightweight LiDAR-Based Cone Detection Framework Using Random Forest for Formula Student Driverless
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 5th International Conference on Cognitive Mobility (CogMob 2026)
summary: Reliable, low-latency perception is crucial for Formula Student Driverless vehicles, yet many existing pipelines rely on deep learning and multi-sensor fusion, often requiring GPU acceleration. This paper presents a lightweight LiDAR-only perception pipeline tailored for CPU execution, combining ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification. Feature importance analysis reduced the model input from 12 to 7 features while preserving performance. Evaluated on 2,371 labeled clusters collected from real FSD events, the pipeline achieves an F1-score of 98.33% and an end-to-end runtime of 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware. The released dataset, labeling tool, and trained models provide a practical and reproducible baseline for other resource-constrained autonomous racing teams.

AI.tldr: A CPU-only LiDAR perception pipeline for Formula Student Driverless racing achieves 98.33% F1-score with 3.13 ms runtime using geometric features and Random Forest classification.
AI.motivation: Existing perception pipelines for autonomous racing rely on deep learning and multi-sensor fusion requiring GPU acceleration, which is unsuitable for resource-constrained platforms. There's a need for lightweight, CPU-only solutions that maintain reliability and low latency for Formula Student Driverless vehicles.
AI.method: Lightweight LiDAR-only pipeline combining ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification. Feature importance analysis reduced input features from 12 to 7 while preserving performance. The system is optimized for CPU execution without GPU acceleration.
AI.result: Achieved 98.33% F1-score on 2,371 labeled clusters from real FSD events with an end-to-end runtime of 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware. Released dataset, labeling tool, and trained models provide a reproducible baseline for resource-constrained teams.
AI.conclusion: The presented CPU-only LiDAR perception pipeline demonstrates that lightweight, geometric feature-based approaches can achieve high performance without GPU acceleration, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained autonomous racing applications while providing valuable open-source resources for the community.

title: A Dataset and Model for Imputing Water Surface Elevation on a Large and Extremely Sparse Spatiotemporal Graph
summary: Continuous monitoring of water surface elevation across river networks is critical for flood forecasting, water resource management, and understanding the global water cycle. Yet, the scarcity of in situ gauges across much of the globe constrains the development of reliable modeling frameworks. Satellite altimetry has the potential to alleviate this problem but its use is currently hindered by sparse temporal coverage. To this end, we introduce AmazonSWE, a dataset for training and evaluating large-scale spatiotemporal graph imputation methods that integrates processed satellite altimetry measurements from a range of sources, including the recent wide-swath SWOT sensor. The dataset covers over 19K river sections and 10 years (2016-2026) in the Amazon river basin, with in situ gauges held out for evaluation. Besides contributing a novel real-world use case with the potential for societal impact, AmazonSWE introduces significant technical challenges: with fewer than 1% of sections observed per day, the dataset is far sparser than existing imputation benchmarks, and its directed acyclic river topology is both structurally different from and larger than graphs in existing datasets. We show that prior spatiotemporal graph imputation methods are not adapted to this topology, scale and sparsity, and propose a simple bidirectional selective state space model that outperforms them by sampling connected subgraphs and flattening space and time into a single token sequence with topology-aware positional encodings. Compared to the state-of-the-art published method for SWOT-based WSE densification, which integrates statistics with physical modeling, our model reduces RMSE against in situ gauges by 18-39%, while producing predictions for every river section rather than only those with sufficient nearby satellite coverage.

AI.tldr: AmazonSWE dataset for spatiotemporal graph imputation in river networks using satellite altimetry, with a new model outperforming existing methods for water surface elevation estimation.
AI.motivation: Global scarcity of in situ water level gauges limits reliable modeling; satellite altimetry has potential but suffers from sparse temporal coverage, creating need for better imputation methods.
AI.method: Created AmazonSWE dataset with 19K+ river sections over 10 years, combining multiple satellite altimetry sources including SWOT. Proposed bidirectional selective state space model with connected subgraph sampling, space-time flattening into tokens, and topology-aware positional encodings.
AI.result: Proposed model reduces RMSE by 18-39% compared to state-of-the-art SWOT-based methods, while providing predictions for all river sections (not just those with satellite coverage). Outperforms prior spatiotemporal graph imputation methods adapted to topology, scale, and sparsity.
AI.conclusion: AmazonSWE enables large-scale river network monitoring with satellite altimetry via improved spatiotemporal imputation, addressing sparse observations and complex river topologies for better water surface elevation estimation.

title: Prompt Revision as a Source of Cultural Bias in Text-to-Image Systems
summary: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before generating images, a step users typically cannot disable or even see. Yet, existing audits of cultural bias examine only the final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, so they cannot tell where the bias originates. We introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. Using it, we audit the revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through a three-step analysis of how heavily it marks each cultural context, whether it flattens that context into a narrow vocabulary, and whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across topically diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. Comparing images from original versus revised prompts on models without a revision layer, we identify the layer itself as a previously undocumented, causal source of this stereotyping. To locate cultural bias, and fix it, we must audit the system as deployed, not the model alone.

AI.tldr: AUDIT reveals text-to-image systems silently revise prompts, introducing cultural bias through marked vocabularies and stereotypes; new WORLDVIEW benchmark enables auditing of this revision layer.
AI.motivation: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before image generation, and existing audits of cultural bias only examine final images without identifying where bias originates in the pipeline.
AI.method: Introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. Audit revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through three-step analysis: 1) measure how heavily it marks each cultural context, 2) whether it flattens context into narrow vocabulary, 3) whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Compare images from original vs. revised prompts.
AI.result: US is least-marked context relative to no-context English baseline. Non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. The revision layer itself is identified as a causal source of stereotyping.
AI.conclusion: To locate and fix cultural bias, we must audit the system as deployed (including revision layers), not just the model alone.

title: LoaDiff: Conditional Generation of Electricity Consumption Time Series for Energy Analytics
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. This paper appeared in IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: The energy transition is reshaping residential electricity consumption through the increasing adoption of distributed generation, electrified appliances, and demand-response programs. Understanding these evolving behaviors requires access to granular smart-meter data for applications such as load forecasting, appliance detection, and demand-side flexibility analysis. However, such data are subject to strict access restrictions and data-protection regulations. Thus, realistic synthetic alternatives are necessary. In this paper, we introduce LoaDiff, a diffusion-based generative model for year-long, sub-hourly smart-meter load curves. LoaDiff supports flexible conditioning on static household attributes, such as appliance ownership, and dynamic contextual variables, including calendar information and outdoor temperature. We evaluate the model against multiple generative baselines on three residential electricity-consumption datasets. Our experiments assess four complementary dimensions: fidelity and diversity, training-record memorization risk, downstream utility for load forecasting and appliance detection, and conditional controllability under alternative temperature conditions. The results show that LoaDiff generates realistic and diverse load profiles, achieves a favorable trade-off between generation quality and limited evidence of memorization, preserves information useful for downstream energy applications, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.

AI.tldr: LoaDiff is a diffusion-based generative model for creating realistic synthetic smart-meter load curves that supports conditioning on household attributes and contextual variables.
AI.motivation: The energy transition is increasing adoption of distributed generation, electrified appliances, and demand-response programs, requiring granular smart-meter data for applications like load forecasting and appliance detection. However, such data face strict access restrictions and data-protection regulations, creating a need for realistic synthetic alternatives.
AI.method: LoaDiff is a diffusion-based generative model that produces year-long, sub-hourly smart-meter load curves with flexible conditioning on static household attributes (like appliance ownership) and dynamic contextual variables (calendar information and outdoor temperature).
AI.result: The model was evaluated against multiple generative baselines on three residential electricity-consumption datasets. Results showed LoaDiff generates realistic and diverse load profiles, achieves favorable trade-off between generation quality and limited memorization risk, preserves information useful for downstream energy applications, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.
AI.conclusion: LoaDiff provides an effective solution for creating synthetic smart-meter data that can support energy research while addressing data privacy concerns, maintaining realistic characteristics for downstream applications, and offering controllable generation based on various conditions.

title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
summary:
Large language model (LLM) training is among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in modern data centers, and power availability is a primary bottleneck to continued AI infrastructure growth. Making the power consumption of these workloads flexible could unlock additional power for AI growth, limit increases in electricity prices, and improve the utilization of existing grid infrastructure. However, to realize this flexibility, we must first understand how the performance of training workloads changes when GPU power is reduced.
  This paper presents the first systematic characterization of \emph{job power elasticity} (the sensitivity of throughput to power reductions) in LLM training. To quantify elasticity, we introduce the \emph{Power Flexibility Index (PFI)}, a normalized metric that quantifies the performance cost of power reductions and provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility.
  We collect data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 (plus 24 H200 validation runs and 34 matched H100 runs), including both dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. We find that LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity, and we identify telemetry signals that predict PFI at runtime. Finally, we demonstrate that PFI-aware power allocation maximizes total tokens/second throughput under power constraints. Under a 30\% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, 63\% of the performance gap between an equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. Our results establish power elasticity as a measurable property of training jobs and provide a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

AI.tldr: LLM training jobs have significant power elasticity (variable performance sensitivity to power reductions), which can be measured with the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) to enable grid-responsive AI infrastructure under power constraints.
AI.motivation: LLM training is rapidly increasing electricity demand in data centers, with power availability becoming a bottleneck for AI growth. Making LLM training power consumption flexible could unlock additional power capacity, limit electricity price increases, and improve grid infrastructure utilization.
AI.method: Introduced the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) to quantify job power elasticity. Collected data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 GPUs (plus validation runs), covering dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining/fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. Identified telemetry signals to predict PFI at runtime.
AI.result: LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity. Under 30% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, achieving 63% of the performance gap between equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. PFI can be predicted using runtime telemetry signals.
AI.conclusion: Power elasticity is a measurable property of training jobs that enables power-aware AI infrastructure. PFI provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility, allowing data centers to respond to grid constraints while optimizing throughput under power limitations.

title: RDDMPI: Residual Denoising Diffusion Model for Probabilistic Multivariate Time Series Imputation
summary: Multivariate time series imputation (MTSI) aims to recover missing values in temporal data composed of multiple interdependent variables. This problem is central to real-world applications such as healthcare monitoring, traffic networks, and energy systems. Recent diffusion-based approaches have shown strong potential for probabilistic imputation by learning to generate missing values through iterative denoising. However, most existing approaches perform diffusion directly in the original data space, requiring the denoising network to simultaneously capture global structure, temporal dynamics, and stochastic variability. This makes the generative task unnecessarily complex, especially when modern deterministic imputers can already provide accurate initial reconstructions. To address this limitation, we propose RDDMPI, a conditional residual diffusion framework that operates directly in residual space. Instead of modeling the full missing signal directly, we reformulate probabilistic imputation as a baseline-residual decomposition, where a pretrained model captures the dominant signal and a diffusion process models the residual uncertainty. To better exploit deterministic guidance, \model{} conditions the reverse denoising process on both the baseline-completed signal and its latent representation, while a reliability-aware conditioning mechanism adaptively controls the influence of baseline information during residual generation. This formulation simplifies the diffusion learning objective, enabling it to focus on structured correction terms rather than reconstructing the full signal. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDDMPI consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: RDDMPI: A conditional residual diffusion framework for multivariate time series imputation that operates in residual space rather than original data space, improving accuracy and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Recent diffusion-based approaches for MTSI perform diffusion directly in original data space, requiring denoising networks to simultaneously capture global structure, temporal dynamics, and stochastic variability. This makes the generative task unnecessarily complex, especially when modern deterministic imputers already provide accurate initial reconstructions.
AI.method: Proposes RDDMPI, a conditional residual diffusion framework that operates in residual space using baseline-residual decomposition. Uses a pretrained model for dominant signal capture and diffusion process for residual uncertainty. Conditions reverse denoising on both baseline-completed signal and its latent representation, with reliability-aware conditioning to adaptively control baseline influence.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show RDDMPI consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating probabilistic imputation as baseline-residual decomposition and operating in residual space, RDDMPI simplifies diffusion learning objectives while achieving better performance in both accuracy and uncertainty modeling for multivariate time series imputation.

title: Enabling Knowledge Graph Understanding at Scale with the EXplore Your Graphs ENgine (EXYGEN)
summary: We present EXYGEN (EXplore Your Graphs ENgine), a framework for knowledge graph (KG) understanding that enables conversational access to KGs at scale. We address two questions in sequence. First, how effectively can LLMs perform text-to-SPARQL generation given only automatically derived structured metadata and small graph samples, rather than task-specific fine-tuning? We integrate VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and ablate KG-derived context on the SciQA benchmark. Our best configuration -- combining ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs -- reaches an exact match of 0.419 on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. We further find that lexical metrics such as F1 poorly predict query correctness, and that larger general-purpose LLMs can outperform smaller code-specialized ones once given sufficient context. Second, we ask how to generate the structured metadata that this method relies on from very large KGs, where KG metadata generation becomes computationally intractable. We introduce a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy that preserves structural diversity while remaining computationally tractable. On OpenCitations Meta and GESIS, it retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x; on ORKG, sampling is not just faster but the only tractable path to obtain complete metadata. Together, these results show that structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs, though closing the remaining gap to fully fine-tuned approaches will likely require reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars -- whether through synthetic generation or an execution-feedback-driven approach -- and validating these findings beyond a single benchmark.

AI.tldr: EXYGEN framework enables conversational access to knowledge graphs using LLMs with structured metadata and graph sampling, achieving 0.419 exact match on SciQA without fine-tuning, plus efficient metadata generation via predicate-coverage-aware sampling.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable conversational access to knowledge graphs without task-specific fine-tuning of LLMs, and to address computational intractability of generating structured metadata from very large KGs.
AI.method: Two-part approach: 1) RAG pipeline integrating VoID descriptions, ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs for text-to-SPARQL generation; 2) Predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy for efficient metadata generation from large KGs.
AI.result: Best configuration achieves 0.419 exact match on SciQA benchmark without fine-tuning; sampling reduces runtime by over 80x while preserving high predicate coverage; larger general-purpose LLMs outperform smaller code-specialized ones with sufficient context.
AI.conclusion: Structured schema context and lightweight prompting reduce reliance on fine-tuning for KG conversational access, though gap remains to fully fine-tuned approaches; future work needs to reduce dependence on curated exemplars through synthetic generation or execution-feedback-driven approaches.

title: Musec: MomentUm SpEctral Clipping for Stable Muon-type Training
summary: Muon has emerged as a highly effective optimizer for large language model training, often achieving superior convergence and performance compared with the widely adopted Adam and AdamW optimizers. Nevertheless, Muon is prone to training instability due to its spectral flattening, manifested by loss spikes and unbounded growth of model weights. Existing approaches primarily rely on weight or attention-logit clipping, which require architecture-specific modifications and do not directly address instability across all model components. We propose MomentUm SpEctral Clipping (Musec), which replaces Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping: rather than setting all singular values of the momentum matrix to approximately one, Musec clips singular values that exceed a threshold while preserving the underlying spectral structure of the momentum. Our strategy provides an optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic mechanism for stabilizing Muon training. We further develop Soft Musec, an efficient implementation that uses a smooth spectral saturation function approximated by coupled Newton-Schulz iterations. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for Musec in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first convergence guarantee for Muon-type methods in the nonconvex nonsmooth setting. We provide empirical studies to show that Soft Musec consistently improves training stability over existing Muon variants across a wide range of learning rates and model sizes. Notably, Soft Musec remains stable in settings where existing Muon variants diverge, while matching their performance under well-tuned configurations.

AI.tldr: Musec stabilizes Muon optimizer training by replacing spectral flattening with spectral clipping, preventing instability while maintaining performance across various model sizes and learning rates.
AI.motivation: Muon optimizer shows superior performance for LLM training but suffers from instability due to spectral flattening, causing loss spikes and weight growth. Existing solutions require architecture-specific modifications and don't fully address instability across all components.
AI.method: Proposes MomentUm SpEctral Clipping (Musec) which replaces Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping that thresholds excessive singular values while preserving momentum structure. Also develops Soft Musec with smooth saturation via Newton-Schulz iterations.
AI.result: Musec provides architecture-agnostic stabilization, maintains performance in stable conditions, and prevents divergence in unstable settings. Establishes first convergence guarantees for Muon-type methods in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization.
AI.conclusion: Musec effectively solves Muon's instability issues through spectral clipping, offering theoretical guarantees and practical stability improvements without compromising performance, making it a robust optimizer choice for LLM training.

title: Making Alternative Data Work: Context-Augmented LLMs for Financial Forecasting
summary: When forecasting a firm's future financial performance, alternative data - data collected from non-traditional sources such as consumer transactions, web traffic, and prediction markets - can provide timely signals about firms' operating activities and broader market conditions. These signals may reveal information that is not captured by traditional public sources and can therefore provide complementary information for forecasting firms' future financial performance. However, firm-level alternative data often have limited historical coverage, are relevant only to specific prediction targets or subsets of firms, and are distributed across numerous heterogeneous channels, making them difficult to incorporate flexibly into conventional forecasting approaches. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) can interpret instructions, learn from in-context examples, and generate predictions by combining heterogeneous information without task-specific parameter updates. Motivated by this potential flexibility, we investigate whether an LLM can forecast firm performance by integrating alternative data with other financial information through in-context learning. We propose a two-agent framework that first identifies the firms for which each alternative data channel is likely to be informative and then predicts revenue using firm- and channel-specific context. We evaluate the framework across four commercial alternative data channels. In our experiments, adding alternative data in context alongside other financial information improves the LLM's forecasting relative to either source alone, and these forecasts are more accurate than those of standard forecasting baselines. These findings suggest that LLMs provide a flexible and practical approach to integrating alternative data with heterogeneous financial information.

AI.tldr: LLMs can effectively integrate alternative data (consumer transactions, web traffic, etc.) with traditional financial information for revenue forecasting using in-context learning, outperforming standard methods.
AI.motivation: Alternative data provides timely signals about firms' operations and market conditions that traditional sources miss, but it suffers from limited historical coverage, specificity to certain firms/targets, and distribution across heterogeneous channels, making it difficult to incorporate into conventional forecasting approaches.
AI.method: A two-agent framework: first identifies which firms each alternative data channel is informative for, then predicts revenue using firm- and channel-specific context through LLM in-context learning, evaluating across four commercial alternative data channels.
AI.result: Adding alternative data alongside other financial information improves LLM forecasting accuracy compared to either source alone, and these forecasts are more accurate than standard forecasting baselines.
AI.conclusion: LLMs provide a flexible and practical approach to integrating alternative data with heterogeneous financial information for firm performance forecasting.

title: Learnware and AI Model Management System
summary: The transition from file storage to database management systems transformed stored data into managed resources. AI now faces an analogous transition from AI model storage to AI model management. Existing model pools essentially serve as \textit{AI model storage systems}. What is needed instead are \textit{AI model management systems} that enable models trained by different developers, for different tasks, with different data, and under different objectives to be identified, reused, and even assembled to address future user tasks. Because AI model developers are generally unwilling to share their training data, such systems should operate without accessing the training data of model developers and, ideally, without accessing raw data of future users. This requirement poses a fundamental challenge: the functionality of a modern AI model may not be fully understood even by the developer who trained it. How, then, can a system identify which models are useful for a given user task, let alone assemble models developed independently for different purposes? At first glance, this objective may appear unattainable. It becomes possible, however, by upgrading the basic unit of management from a machine learning model to a \textit{learnware}. \textit{Learnware = Model + Specification}. The specification, whose assignment transforms a trained model into a learnware, is generated with the help of a machine learning process without disclosing the training data of the developer and has a theoretically established data-preservation property. The \textit{Learnware Dock System (LDS)} provides a path toward powerful AI model management systems. Because specifications are generated according to a published reference and are comparable across models, they can also serve as an AI model \textit{collaboration protocol} through which independently developed models, including intelligent agents, can collaborate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes transforming AI model storage into AI model management systems through "learnwares" - models with specifications that enable model reuse and collaboration without accessing training data.
AI.motivation: Existing AI model pools function as storage systems rather than management systems. There's a need for systems that can identify, reuse, and assemble independently developed models for new user tasks, without accessing proprietary training data or user raw data.
AI.method: Introduces the concept of "learnwares" = Model + Specification. The specification is generated via machine learning processes without disclosing training data, has data-preservation properties, and enables comparison across models. Proposes the Learnware Dock System (LDS) as an implementation framework.
AI.result: Learnwares enable AI model management where models can be identified and assembled for new tasks without accessing training data. Specifications serve as a collaboration protocol that allows independently developed models and intelligent agents to work together.
AI.conclusion: The transition from AI model storage to AI model management systems is achievable through learnwares, addressing the fundamental challenge of reusing and assembling independently developed AI models while preserving data privacy.

title: Distributed Optimization of Modular Production Systems using Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Inverse Models
summary: This paper presents a novel approach for data-driven self-learning control of highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems. Specifically, we employ a novel framework for model-based reinforcement learning which introduces approximate inverse process models within the training of reinforcement policies. This approach disentangles the learning of actuation dynamics and the dynamics in state space, resulting in RL-based training solely within the task space. We propose a lightweight feedforward architecture for approximate inverse models and integrate them within the policy network of standard RL algorithms. We apply the approach to a laboratory modular production testbed with heterogeneous production modules. The results underline the efficiency improvements for modular manufacturing units in terms of both performance and training speed, particularly for off-policy algorithms.

AI.tldr: A novel model-based reinforcement learning framework using approximate inverse process models for self-learning control of modular manufacturing systems, enabling RL training solely in task space rather than state space.
AI.motivation: The need for efficient data-driven control of highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems that can adapt to heterogeneous production modules without extensive manual tuning.
AI.method: Proposes a framework that introduces approximate inverse process models into RL training, disentangling actuation dynamics from state space dynamics. Uses lightweight feedforward architectures for inverse models integrated into standard RL policy networks.
AI.result: Demonstrated efficiency improvements for modular manufacturing units in both performance and training speed, with particular benefits for off-policy RL algorithms, validated on a laboratory modular production testbed.
AI.conclusion: The approximate inverse model approach successfully enables effective RL-based control for complex modular manufacturing systems by simplifying the learning problem to task space, offering practical benefits for industrial automation.

title: Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work?
summary: Post-training quantization compresses large language models (LLMs) by storing their weights at reduced precision, and each quantized weight introduces an error into the hidden states. Naively, these errors should accumulate with depth and corrupt next-token prediction; randomly initialized models accumulate these discrepancies rapidly, whereas quantized pretrained models accumulate much less hidden-state error and largely maintain downstream task performance, even though they were never trained with quantization noise. This raises the question we address: why does post-training quantization work? Comparing full-precision and quantized forward passes, we identify two mechanisms that characterize pretrained quantization robustness. First, the error a layer newly introduces tends to oppose the error it inherits from the layer's input. The two cancel partially such that the discrepancy between full-precision and quantized passes grows slowly. This counteracting residual interaction develops during pretraining. Our quantitative analysis identifies it as a major factor slowing hidden-error growth. Second, LM-head geometry preferentially preserves the scores and probabilities of high-ranked tokens, which typically represent the model's most confident predictions. Together, these mechanisms explain why quantization error that passes through numerous layers can still produce only small output changes, and we verify the findings across models and quantization settings.

AI.tldr: Post-training quantization works for LLMs because pretraining develops error-canceling mechanisms between layers and LM-head geometry preserves high-ranked tokens, explaining why quantization noise doesn't corrupt predictions despite passing through many layers.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a puzzling observation: post-training quantization introduces weight errors that should accumulate with network depth and corrupt predictions, yet quantized pretrained models maintain performance while randomly initialized models fail rapidly. This paradox raises the fundamental question of why post-training quantization works for pretrained LLMs despite no quantization-specific training.
AI.method: The authors compare full-precision and quantized forward passes to identify mechanisms behind quantization robustness. They analyze error propagation through layers, examining how quantization errors accumulate or cancel. They also investigate LM-head geometry's effect on preserving token probabilities. Quantitative analysis is conducted across models and quantization settings to verify findings.
