AI.result: Two key mechanisms are identified: 1) Pretraining develops counteracting residual interactions where each layer's newly introduced quantization error tends to oppose inherited input error, causing partial cancellation and slow error growth. 2) LM-head geometry preferentially preserves scores and probabilities of high-ranked tokens (model's most confident predictions). These mechanisms explain why quantization error passing through numerous layers produces only small output changes.
AI.conclusion: Post-training quantization works for pretrained LLMs due to error-canceling properties developed during pretraining and geometric properties of the LM head that protect high-confidence predictions. These emergent properties explain quantization robustness without quantization-specific training, providing fundamental understanding of why weight errors don't catastrophically accumulate in practice.

title: MAPLE: Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution
summary: Domain practitioners understand their business constraints but may lack operations-research expertise or dedicated support. LLM-based optimization agents translate natural-language requirements into models or solver programs that established optimization tools can execute. This progress makes optimization more accessible, but real-world operations are dynamic: changing demand, resources, and priorities require updates to data, constraints, and objectives. Methods centered on isolated requests offer limited support for rapid adaptation that preserves earlier decisions and reuses useful search results. We introduce MAPLE (Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution), an agent for maintaining optimization problems through successive natural-language requests. MAPLE combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It retains the optimization program, accepted plans, earlier updates, and candidate solutions for subsequent requests. We introduce NLDO, a benchmark of 15 trajectories and 180 updates spanning selection, scheduling, rostering, routing, and cloud-resource placement. In the main evaluation, MAPLE completes all trajectories and achieves online scalar quality of 0.951 and a Pareto hypervolume ratio of 0.875. Controlled comparisons further show that maintaining executable state improves update validity and can preserve useful search information across substantial revisions.

AI.tldr: MAPLE is a memory-augmented LLM-based optimization agent that handles successive natural-language requests to maintain and update optimization problems, combining language processing with mathematical programming and evolutionary search while retaining program state and previous solutions.
AI.motivation: Real-world operations are dynamic with changing demand, resources, and priorities that require frequent updates to optimization problems. Current LLM-based optimization methods focused on isolated requests offer limited support for rapid adaptation while preserving earlier decisions and reusing search results.
AI.method: MAPLE combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It maintains memory of the optimization program, accepted plans, earlier updates, and candidate solutions to handle successive natural-language requests. The system was evaluated using NLDO benchmark with 15 trajectories and 180 updates across various optimization domains.
AI.result: MAPLE completed all trajectories in the NLDO benchmark, achieving online scalar quality of 0.951 and Pareto hypervolume ratio of 0.875. Controlled comparisons showed that maintaining executable state improves update validity and preserves useful search information across substantial revisions.
AI.conclusion: MAPLE successfully addresses the need for maintaining optimization problems through successive updates, demonstrating that memory-augmented approaches can effectively support dynamic real-world optimization by preserving state and reusing search results across multiple requests.

title: Predicting Privacy Leakage from Weight Spectral Density
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are widely used to audit the privacy disclosure risk of machine learning models, however current state-of-the-art attacks require training computationally expensive shadow models, making large-scale privacy evaluation impractical. In this work, we investigate whether inexpensive spectral metrics derived from the heavy-tailed self-regularisation framework can serve as proxies for MIA vulnerability. We evaluate several WeightWatcher spectral metrics on image and tabular classification tasks and compare their relationship with MIA privacy leakage against conventional measures of generalisation. Across datasets, stable rank exhibits a strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows a consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability at the low false-positive regime. These associations are observed to be stronger than those obtained using the generalisation gap. The results indicate that neural network spectra may contain information about privacy leakage that is not fully captured by conventional measures of overfitting, motivating spectral analysis as a promising direction for scalable privacy auditing.

AI.tldr: Heavy-tailed spectral metrics from neural network weight matrices can serve as efficient proxies for membership inference attack vulnerability, with stable rank showing strong positive correlation and Log alpha-Norm showing negative correlation with privacy leakage.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art membership inference attacks require training computationally expensive shadow models, making large-scale privacy evaluation impractical. The authors aim to find inexpensive spectral metrics that can serve as proxies for MIA vulnerability without needing expensive shadow model training.
AI.method: The authors evaluate several WeightWatcher spectral metrics (from the heavy-tailed self-regularization framework) on both image and tabular classification tasks. They analyze the relationship between these spectral metrics and MIA privacy leakage, comparing against conventional measures of generalization like generalization gap.
AI.result: Stable rank exhibits strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability in the low false-positive regime. These associations are stronger than those obtained using the generalization gap, indicating spectral metrics capture privacy leakage information not fully captured by conventional overfitting measures.
AI.conclusion: Neural network spectral analysis provides a promising direction for scalable privacy auditing, as spectral metrics contain information about privacy leakage that conventional overfitting measures miss, enabling more efficient privacy vulnerability assessment without expensive shadow model training.

title: Autonomy, Social Norms, and Alignment: Towards a Developmental Framework for Autonomous Artificial Agents
comment: In publication in the proceedings of SIpEIA 2026 conference
summary: In recent years, artificial intelligence has made extraordinary progress thanks to large-scale models capable of generalization and the generation of complex outputs. However, transferring this potential into embodied agents reveals a significant limitation: the most advanced systems rely on pre-existing datasets and human feedback strategies that are powerful but insufficient in dynamic or unknown contexts. To adapt, an agent must acquire knowledge through direct interaction with its environment. One strategy to address this challenge involves introducing higher-level mechanisms, such as intrinsic motivations, which leverage curiosity and competence, to guide exploration and learning in complex environments. While this flexibility expands autonomy, it complicates the task of ensuring agents remain aligned with human goals. Alignment, already a challenge for artificial systems in general, becomes even more complex in unstructured and dynamic contexts where predefined rules prove insufficient. To be effective and adaptable, norms must be rooted in experience through an epistemological process that starting from simple, situated principles allows for the gradual construction of more complex rules through experience, autonomous learning, and cooperation with other moral agents. Similarly to children learning social norms by exploring their environment and participating in collective practices, artificial agents must also be educated toward alignment. Following Dennett, the status of a moral agent is not innate but is attributed gradually based on the ability to responsibly manage increasing degrees of freedom. From this perspective, the regulatory sandboxes can be viewed as pedagogical environments for AI: dynamic spaces where alignment develops as a formative process, progressively shaping autonomous behaviors through interaction and cooperation in scenarios of increasing complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI systems lack embodied adaptability to dynamic environments, proposing that alignment should be an educational process where AI agents develop moral norms through experience, intrinsic motivation, and cooperation in regulatory sandboxes, similar to how children learn social norms.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the limitation of current large-scale AI models that rely on pre-existing datasets and human feedback, which are insufficient for embodied agents operating in dynamic or unknown contexts where agents must acquire knowledge through direct interaction.
AI.method: The proposed method involves using intrinsic motivations (curiosity and competence) to guide exploration, coupled with an epistemological process where norms are constructed gradually from simple principles through experience, autonomous learning, and cooperation with other moral agents in regulatory sandboxes.
AI.result: The paper conceptualizes regulatory sandboxes as pedagogical environments where AI alignment develops as a formative process, progressively shaping autonomous behaviors through interaction and cooperation in increasingly complex scenarios, analogous to how children learn social norms.
AI.conclusion: AI alignment should be viewed as an educational process rather than a fixed objective, where artificial agents gradually earn moral agency status through responsible management of increasing autonomy in structured learning environments, drawing inspiration from developmental psychology and Dennett's philosophy of moral agency.

title: Dynamic language model representations for multi-objective reaction optimisation
summary: Optimising chemical reactions across multiple objectives, such as yield, selectivity, and safety, is central to chemical synthesis, and model-driven approaches depend critically on how reaction components are represented. Established featurisations are either chemically uninformative, as with one-hot encodings, or, as with molecular descriptors, do not readily extend across chemically distinct components. For structurally and functionally diverse components, it is therefore unclear what a shared representation should contain. Constructing such a representation is itself a challenging research undertaking that must be revisited for each new reaction system. Here we bypass this step by learning the reaction representation dynamically from text. Textual descriptions of reaction conditions are encoded by a fine-tuned language model trained jointly with Gaussian process surrogates, yielding task-adaptive representations within a multi-objective Bayesian optimisation loop. Across nickel- and palladium-catalysed cross-couplings in both sequential and parallel experimentation regimes, this approach reaches optimisation convergence in fewer experiments than descriptor libraries or one-hot encoding. Applied prospectively to a palladium-catalysed cyanation spanning mixed ligand denticity and heterogeneous additives, and to a three-objective asymmetric hydrogenation across chiral iridium and ruthenium catalyst families, two rounds of high-throughput experimentation (192 reactions, under 3% of each design space) delivered conditions translating directly to gram scale in 94% and 84% isolated yield, the latter at 99.6% enantiomeric excess.

AI.tldr: Language model-learned text representations of reaction conditions outperform traditional featurizations in multi-objective Bayesian optimization of chemical reactions, achieving optimal conditions with fewer experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing chemical reaction representations (one-hot encodings or molecular descriptors) are either chemically uninformative or don't generalize well across diverse reaction components, requiring system-specific representation development for each new reaction.
AI.method: Fine-tuned language model encodes textual descriptions of reaction conditions, trained jointly with Gaussian process surrogates within a multi-objective Bayesian optimization loop to create task-adaptive representations.
AI.result: Approach converges faster than traditional methods in nickel- and palladium-catalyzed cross-couplings. Applied to palladium-catalyzed cyanation and asymmetric hydrogenation, 192 reactions (under 3% of design space) delivered conditions yielding 94% and 84% isolated yields, the latter with 99.6% enantiomeric excess.
AI.conclusion: Text-based representation learning dynamically from language models provides a general, effective alternative to manual feature engineering for chemical reaction optimization, enabling efficient multi-objective optimization across diverse reaction systems.

title: Geospatial AI, Dataverse Metadata, and the Study of Place-Based Government
summary: Harvard Dataverse hosts over 150,000 research datasets, but the geographic information those datasets carry is entered as free text by depositors and has never been assembled into a searchable structure. We construct a knowledge graph from the repository's public data and metadata, organizing 102,650 datasets within a 215,985-node network of 528,003 edges linking datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations. Of those datasets, 43,991 (42.9 percent) carry at least one geospatial field, geographic coverage, geographic unit, or a bounding box and 96.9 percent of all nodes sit in a single connected component, so datasets remain reachable from one another even when their geospatial metadata share nothing in common. A conservative keyword search identifies 7,654 geospatially tagged datasets (17.4 percent) as directly policy-relevant, with elections and legislatures the largest cluster, followed by government administration, health policy, transportation, and education. Five datasets illustrate how this metadata behaves across policy domains and spatial scales, and an extended use case shows how community language models, stance detection with geographic aggregation, and partisan language bridging tools can attach discourse to place. The central obstacle is place resolution: the same location appears as many disconnected nodes. We argue that the graph provides a concrete setting for developing AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution, and we document its coverage skew toward American, city-level data.

AI.tldr: Researchers built a knowledge graph from Harvard Dataverse metadata, connecting 102,650 datasets to keywords, publications, and locations, revealing significant geospatial content and policy relevance while highlighting challenges with place name resolution.
AI.motivation: Harvard Dataverse hosts over 150,000 research datasets with geographic information entered as free text, making it unsearchable and disconnected. There's a need to organize this geospatial metadata into a structured, searchable format to enable discovery and analysis of policy-relevant datasets.
AI.method: Constructed a knowledge graph from repository's public data and metadata, organizing datasets into a network with nodes and edges linking datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations. Used conservative keyword search to identify policy-relevant datasets and examined how metadata behaves across policy domains and spatial scales.
AI.result: Created a 215,985-node network with 528,003 edges linking 102,650 datasets. Found 43,991 datasets (42.9%) have geospatial metadata, with 96.9% of nodes in a single connected component. Identified 7,654 datasets (17.4% of geospatial ones) as directly policy-relevant, with elections/legislatures as largest cluster. Discovered coverage skew toward American, city-level data.
AI.conclusion: The knowledge graph provides a concrete setting for developing AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution. The main challenge is place resolution (same locations appear as disconnected nodes), and the graph reveals systematic coverage biases while enabling new approaches to attach discourse to place through language models and stance detection.

title: Thinking with Looped Flows
summary: Humans and machines often solve harder problems by spending more time on computation. In deep learning, looped models implement this idea during inference by recurrently updating a hidden state. In practice, however, their training backpropagates through only one or a few updates, making it hard to train early updates to support future ones. We propose looped flows, an approach that sidesteps this issue by training the recurrence with local denoising objectives. By imposing temporal association across denoising objectives through progressively decreasing noise levels and shared noise, the model is incentivized to learn recurrent states that transfer useful computation over time, even when gradients cover only a few updates. We then formulate inference as integrating the velocity of a probability flow parameterized by the learned denoiser, coupled with recurrent states. This allows solving harder problems by spending more computation through a finer temporal grid and enables multiple valid predictions from different initial noise samples. Across six reasoning benchmarks including two multi-solution benchmarks, looped flows outperform prior state-of-the-art looped models overall, achieving 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2.

AI.tldr: Looped Flows: A method that trains recurrent neural networks with local denoising objectives and temporal association to enable effective long-range computation during inference, achieving state-of-the-art performance on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current looped models in deep learning are limited because their training backpropagates through only one or few recurrent updates, making it difficult to train early updates to support future ones. This prevents effective long-range computation during inference.
AI.method: Proposes looped flows that train recurrence with local denoising objectives. Uses temporal association across denoising objectives through progressively decreasing noise levels and shared noise. Formulates inference as integrating probability flow velocity parameterized by the learned denoiser with recurrent states.
AI.result: Outperforms prior state-of-the-art looped models across six reasoning benchmarks, achieving 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2. Enables solving harder problems with more computation via finer temporal grid and generates multiple valid predictions from different initial noise.
AI.conclusion: Looped flows successfully address the gradient limitation in training recurrent models by using local denoising objectives with temporal association, enabling effective long-range computation during inference and achieving strong performance on challenging reasoning tasks.

title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can benefit from reusable skills distilled from prior task experience, yet existing skill optimization methods often rely on costly execution-based evaluation and substantial task data. We introduce \textbf{COBRA-Skills}, an efficient framework that formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. COBRA-Skills couples contextual-bandit-guided prioritization with evidence-grounded skill evolution, selectively allocating evaluations to promising or informative candidates while continually refining the skill population from execution feedback. Across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, COBRA-Skills consistently achieves the strongest average performance among compared methods, while reducing optimization cost by 55--58\% relative to SkillOpt and using only 50 unique optimization examples per benchmark. Further analyses show that COBRA-Skills remains robust to changes in the agent harness and performs effectively when the target model itself is used for skill generation and refinement.

AI.tldr: COBRA-Skills is an efficient LLM agent skill optimization framework using contextual bandits and evidence-based evolution, achieving strong performance while reducing optimization costs by 55-58%.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent skill optimization methods are costly, requiring extensive execution-based evaluation and substantial task data. There's a need for more efficient approaches that can distill reusable skills from prior experience without high computational overhead.
AI.method: COBRA-Skills formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. It combines contextual-bandit-guided prioritization (to selectively allocate evaluations to promising candidates) with evidence-grounded skill evolution (to refine the skill population from execution feedback).
AI.result: The framework achieves the strongest average performance across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, while reducing optimization cost by 55-58% relative to SkillOpt. It uses only 50 unique optimization examples per benchmark and remains robust to agent harness changes and works effectively when the target model handles skill generation and refinement.
AI.conclusion: COBRA-Skills provides an efficient and effective framework for LLM agent skill optimization, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining or improving performance compared to existing methods.

title: Model-Aware Schedules Improve Generation via Fiberwise Optimal Transport
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Keywords: Diffusion models; flow matching; schedule optimization; fiberwise optimal transport; time reparameterization; empirical universality
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching schedules control the signal and noise coefficients that mix data and noise along affine probability paths. Minimizing a kinetic action defined on coefficient paths, motivated by optimal transport, helps explain strong baselines but remains model-agnostic and ignores prediction error. Here we introduce a model-aware schedule construction based on fiberwise optimal transport. At a fixed time and state on the probability path, compatible signal/noise decompositions form an affine fiber. We define a fiberwise prediction risk by averaging optimal-transport costs between the true and predictor-induced decompositions within these fibers. On a fixed coefficient curve, combining this risk with coefficient-path kinetic action yields a closed-form optimal time allocation. This construction extends to general linear prediction targets, and the risk profile can be estimated from an early baseline checkpoint. We evaluate DDPMs and flow matching across prediction targets, training configurations, risk-estimation checkpoints, datasets, and architectures. Our model-aware schedules consistently outperform strong baselines, including a 38.6% relative FID reduction for flow matching on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations. Each model-agnostic kinetic baseline determines its own kinetic reference coordinate. In these coordinates, fiberwise-risk profiles from independently trained models in different settings align closely after normalization to unit area. The resulting schedule deformations used in training also align, suggesting empirical universality across the evaluated models and settings. Pretrained-checkpoint diagnostics extend this normalized-risk agreement to larger conditional latent diffusion and 2-RF models. A frozen analytic allocation template retains most of the model-aware improvement without further risk estimation or model-specific fitting.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces model-aware schedule construction for diffusion/flow-matching based on fiberwise optimal transport, achieving better performance than model-agnostic baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing schedule optimization methods based on minimizing kinetic action are model-agnostic and ignore prediction error, limiting their effectiveness.
AI.method: Uses fiberwise optimal transport to define prediction risk within affine fibers of signal/noise decompositions, combining this risk with kinetic action for closed-form optimal time allocation. Risk profiles can be estimated from early checkpoints.
AI.result: Model-aware schedules consistently outperform strong baselines, with 38.6% relative FID reduction for flow matching on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations. Shows empirical universality across models/settings with aligned risk profiles.
AI.conclusion: Fiberwise optimal transport provides effective model-aware schedule optimization, with risk profiles showing universal patterns across different models and settings, enabling improved performance without extensive model-specific fitting.

title: AdamX: Cosine similarity meets gradient descent
summary: We introduce AdamX, a first-order optimizer that incorporates cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes. The proposed method is scalable, model-agnostic, and straightforward to integrate into existing training pipelines. We further introduce a variance rectification scheme that promotes smoother optimization during the early stages of training. Overall, we provide empirical evidence that AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across a range of benchmark datasets and architectures. Performance is evaluated in terms of the number of epochs required to reach predefined performance thresholds under a fixed hyperparameter budget. Code and Experiments available at: https://github.com/FranciscoCaldas/adamX.

AI.tldr: AdamX is a first-order optimizer that uses cosine similarity to adaptively control update magnitudes with a variance rectification scheme for smoother early training, achieving competitive convergence rates across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to improve upon existing optimization methods by developing a more adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes during neural network training, potentially leading to better convergence behavior.
AI.method: AdamX incorporates cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes and includes a variance rectification scheme to promote smoother optimization during early training stages. It's designed to be scalable, model-agnostic, and easy to integrate into existing pipelines.
AI.result: Empirical evidence shows AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across a range of benchmark datasets and architectures. Performance is evaluated based on epochs required to reach predefined performance thresholds under fixed hyperparameter budgets.
AI.conclusion: AdamX is an effective first-order optimizer that demonstrates competitive performance through its cosine similarity-based adaptive update mechanism and variance rectification scheme, making it a viable alternative to existing optimization methods.

title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the Industry Track of EMNLP 2026
summary: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

AI.tldr: SIRF is a risk foundation model that internalizes platform policies through continued pretraining, achieving high-precision risk detection with ultra-low latency, outperforming similar-sized models while maintaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Industrial content risk control requires high precision and second-level latency, not just average accuracy. Current systems need to automatically handle risks while applying complex platform policies accurately under strict time constraints.
AI.method: 1) Internalize platform policies using EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting, and account-level chain-of-thought synthesis without additional human annotation. 2) Use continued pretraining (CPT) to encode policies into model weights. 3) Deploy as verdict-only system for ultra-low latency. 4) Compare with baseline (Qwen3-8B-SFT) using same policy injection and output form to isolate internalization effect.
AI.result: SIRF-8B-SFT achieves 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1 percentage points improvement over baseline. Uses only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability. Matches or exceeds larger systems in logprob-available models. Enables tree-model adjudication (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to freezing scenarios with ~70% relative mis-penalization reduction.
AI.conclusion: SIRF successfully internalizes complex platform policies through continued pretraining, enabling high-precision risk control with ultra-low latency. The approach improves risk detection while maintaining model generality, making it suitable for industrial deployment in content risk control systems.

title: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables AI systems to turn experience and feedback into persistent changes that improve both their capabilities and the process of future improvement. We first use the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI) to reveal the problems of existing LLMs, then introduce the RSI concept and its development roadmap: from improvement-execution autonomy, improvement-strategy autonomy, experience-acquisition autonomy, and environment-adaptation autonomy, to recursive meta-improvement. Next we examine RSI across scenarios (e.g., scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, software engineering), highlighting their distinct requirements and development speeds. Drawing on diverse industry practices and preliminary empirical evidence, we connect RSI research with practical systems and identify key challenges to achieving genuine RSI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) as a framework for AI systems to continuously improve both their capabilities and improvement processes through various autonomy levels, examines RSI across different application scenarios, and identifies key practical challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs have limitations as revealed by the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI), motivating the need for a more systematic approach to AI improvement. The paper aims to establish a conceptual framework for RSI that addresses how AI systems can persistently enhance themselves through experience and feedback loops.
AI.method: The paper introduces a hierarchical RSI development roadmap with five levels of autonomy: improvement-execution, improvement-strategy, experience-acquisition, environment-adaptation, and recursive meta-improvement. It examines RSI across different scenarios (scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, software engineering), analyzes industry practices, and uses preliminary empirical evidence to identify practical implementation challenges.
AI.result: The paper presents a structured conceptual framework for RSI with distinct autonomy levels, identifies different RSI requirements and development speeds across application scenarios, connects theoretical RSI research with practical systems, and highlights key implementation challenges for achieving genuine recursive self-improvement.
AI.conclusion: RSI represents a crucial advancement in AI development, offering a systematic pathway for AI systems to achieve persistent self-improvement across multiple autonomy dimensions. However, significant practical challenges remain in implementing genuine RSI systems, requiring further research and development across different application domains.

title: A Unified Per-Token Gating Family for On-Policy Distillation: FKL/RKL Mixing with Multi-Channel and Bias Coefficients
comment: Accepted at the Findings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026 Findings)
summary: Per-token gating of forward/reverse KL losses has become a standard technique for on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), but existing methods such as EOPD (Jin et al., 2026) and ToDi (Jung et al., 2025) each fix a single gating signal and a single gating direction, and the two have never been compared directly. We introduce a four-coefficient parameterization lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t) in which direction-aligned proxies of EOPD and ToDi appear as one-dimensional (1D) restrictions, and which adds multi-channel composition and an explicit bias as further degrees of freedom. On TweetEval (Barbieri et al., 2020) emotion and hate, with a Qwen3-32B teacher and a Qwen3-4B student, configurations in the full family reach higher accuracy than the matched-magnitude single-channel (entropy-only / gap-only) 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells, and a 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment places dynamic gating ahead of effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Because cells share training data, models, and parameter substructure, we report both counts as exploratory aggregate directional evidence rather than as independent hypothesis tests. Targeted three-seed paired replications of the nine headline comparisons singled out by that sweep -- including a third task, offensive -- are directionally consistent, but individually smaller than the single-seed estimates and not significant at n=3. We therefore present the parameterization primarily as a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD.

AI.tldr: A new four-coefficient parameterization for per-token gating in on-policy knowledge distillation that unifies and extends existing methods (EOPD and ToDi), showing improved performance over single-channel baselines across multiple classification tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing per-token gating methods for on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD) like EOPD and ToDi each use a single fixed gating signal and direction, and have never been directly compared. There's a need for a unified framework that can encompass and extend these approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce a four-coefficient parameterization λ_t = σ(a·h_t + b·u(x) + c + d·gap_t) where: h_t is token entropy, u(x) is a task-specific baseline, gap_t is the KL gap, and σ is the sigmoid. This formulation allows EOPD and ToDi as one-dimensional restrictions, while adding multi-channel composition and explicit bias as additional degrees of freedom.
AI.result: On TweetEval emotion and hate classification tasks with Qwen3-32B teacher and Qwen3-4B student: 1) Configurations in the full family outperformed matched-magnitude single-channel restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells; 2) A 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment showed dynamic gating outperformed effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Three-seed replications of key comparisons were directionally consistent but not statistically significant at n=3.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parameterization provides a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD, unifying existing approaches and offering improved performance through multi-channel composition and explicit bias terms. Results suggest dynamic gating has advantages over static baselines, though more replication is needed for statistical significance.

title: CoRA-NAS: Coarse Ranking and Anchor-Residual Refinement for Neural Architecture Search
summary: Zero-cost proxies rank architectures cheaply, but their reliability varies across search spaces. We introduce CoRA-NAS (COarse Ranking + Anchor-residual), a two-stage framework combining a static ranking prior with low-cost learning-curve refinement. CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies through an equal-weight log-rank consensus and a target-free consensus gate. CoRA-Refine samples anchors across this prior, extrapolates their early validation curves, and propagates a learned residual correction with an ExtraTrees model. The refinement uses approximately 1% of the cost of fully training the candidate set. Fully trained architecture-accuracy labels are not used to fit the ranker. One configuration is used across spaces, with space-specific architecture encodings. Across NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101, TransNAS-Bench-101, and NATS-SSS, CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894, respectively. Its worst-space correlation of 0.715 is the highest among the compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, its selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, near the reported ground-truth best of 73.37%. On the pure size space, refinement recovers the static prior's shortfall relative to parameter count, while remaining tied with the strongest capacity proxies within noise. The resulting framework combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection.

AI.tldr: CoRA-NAS is a two-stage NAS framework combining static ranking proxies with low-cost learning-curve refinement, achieving strong cross-space correlation with only ~1% training cost.
AI.motivation: Zero-cost proxies for neural architecture search are cheap but unreliable across different search spaces, needing more robust and cost-effective ranking methods.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: CoRA-Rank aggregates multiple zero-cost proxies using equal-weight log-rank consensus, then CoRA-Refine samples anchor architectures, extrapolates early learning curves, and applies ExtraTrees model residual correction with only ~1% training cost.
AI.result: Achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894 across four benchmarks; worst-space correlation of 0.715 is highest among compared methods; achieves 73.32% accuracy on NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100 (near ground-truth best 73.37%).
AI.conclusion: CoRA-NAS provides cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost refinement, effectively combining static proxies with minimal training for accurate architecture selection.

title: From Parameters to Answers: How LLMs Retrieve and Use Their Internal Knowledge
summary: How does a language model's dependence on query-routing information and target knowledge change as it answers a question? We study this question through layerwise interventions on the hidden state at the end of the question. Across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, we compare country-continent questions with noun, adjective, and code answers while keeping several fitted measurements distinct. A pair-conditioned request direction describes which country is queried in natural single-country questions; a global request direction describes first- versus second-country requests in paired questions; separate selection candidates test control among contents already available in the hidden state. A diagnostic reanalysis of frozen Qwen natural-question states shows that the pair-conditioned direction grows stronger before interventions on it begin to alter later fitted knowledge, with this causal window opening while answer-supporting content is still forming. The paired three-model trajectories are not uniform: Gemma shows a partially overlapping mid-layer routing-content profile, whereas Llama has no sustained routing-effect window under the same gates. In the paired protocol, dependence on the global request direction decreases from fixed earlier to later layer sets while dependence on fitted content persists. A matched Qwen comparison shows that the pair-conditioned direction retains a late effect, so this operational handoff concerns the global fitted direction rather than all request information. These results separate early readability, natural strength, causal steering, and later content dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how language models sequentially use query-routing information and target knowledge while answering questions through layerwise interventions on hidden states, revealing distinct timing patterns in different models.
AI.motivation: The researchers want to understand how language models dynamically rely on different types of information (query routing vs. target knowledge) during question answering, and how this dependence evolves across model layers as they process questions.
AI.method: They conduct layerwise interventions on hidden states at the end of questions across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma models. They use country-continent questions with different answer types while keeping fitted measurements distinct. They analyze: pair-conditioned request direction (which country is queried in single-country questions), global request direction (first vs. second country in paired questions), and separate selection candidates to test control. They perform diagnostic reanalysis of frozen states and compare three models' trajectories.
AI.result: The pair-conditioned direction grows stronger before interventions begin to alter later fitted knowledge, with the causal window opening while answer-supporting content is still forming. Model trajectories differ: Gemma shows partially overlapping routing-content profile, Llama has no sustained routing-effect window under the same gates. Dependence on global request direction decreases from earlier to later layers while dependence on fitted content persists. The pair-conditioned direction retains late effects, indicating operational handoff concerns the global fitted direction rather than all request information.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully separates early readability, natural strength, causal steering, and later content dependence in language models, revealing distinct temporal patterns in how models process and integrate query routing information with target knowledge across different architectures.

title: CausalArena: Benchmarking Causal Discovery in the Foundation Model Era
summary: Causal discovery aims to uncover causal structures from data and is fundamental to scientific reasoning and intervention-based decision making. Its evaluation relies heavily on structural causal models (SCMs), which specify a causal graph together with the mechanisms that generate data, yet existing studies differ substantially in graph families, mechanisms, and evaluation protocols. The emergence of causal discovery foundation models (CDFMs) further complicates evaluation: performance may reflect not only causal discovery ability, but also overlap between pretraining environments and test SCMs, making results on fixed synthetic benchmarks difficult to interpret. We introduce CausalArena, a unified and evolvable benchmark for causal discovery under a common protocol. Synthetic SCMs supply controlled breadth over structures and mechanisms; semantic operational SCMs provide human-auditable, semantically grounded environments beyond standard synthetic generators; and formula-grounded SCMs test discovery under explicit scientific mechanisms. Public real-world datasets provide an additional external-validity check. Experiments across classical, neural, and pretrained methods reveal substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols, showing that strong performance in one benchmark regime does not reliably transfer to others. These results highlight benchmark diversity and pretraining--evaluation overlap as central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era.

AI.tldr: CausalArena is a unified, evolvable benchmark for evaluating causal discovery methods across diverse structural causal model families, addressing evaluation challenges in the foundation model era.
AI.motivation: Current causal discovery evaluation suffers from inconsistent protocols, diverse SCM implementations, and the emerging challenge of foundation models where performance may reflect pretraining-test overlap rather than true causal discovery ability.
AI.method: Created CausalArena benchmark with three SCM types: synthetic (controlled breadth), semantic operational (human-auditable), and formula-grounded (explicit scientific mechanisms), plus real-world datasets for external validity.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols, revealing that strong performance on one benchmark doesn't transfer to others, highlighting the importance of diverse evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark diversity and pretraining-evaluation overlap are central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era, requiring more comprehensive evaluation frameworks like CausalArena.

title: Explainability Assistant: A Conversational XAI Interface for Interpreting Energy Consumption Models
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted author version of a paper published at ICECET 2026
summary: Energy consumption forecasting relies on increasingly complex machine learning (ML) models, such as Genetic Programming-based symbolic regressors, whose predictions can be difficult for facility managers and building operators to interpret. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques address this opacity, but traditional XAI dashboards require substantial technical expertise and provide limited flexibility for dynamic, context-aware inquiry. Conversational XAI systems offer a promising alternative; however, previous approaches, such as TalkToModel, were constrained by rigid custom grammars and achieved only 76.8% intent-parsing accuracy. This paper introduces the Explainability Assistant, an open-source conversational XAI system that leverages the function-calling capabilities of modern Large Language Models (LLMs) to overcome these limitations. The system achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy, supports flexible natural language interaction, and adapts to different ML problem types without task-specific fine-tuning. We present the system's architecture and report results from a comparative evaluation conducted with energy domain specialists, contrasting the Explainability Assistant with a traditional XAI dashboard. The evaluation suggests improved usability and consistent task accuracy, with all experts unanimously preferring the conversational interface for practical use.

AI.tldr: A conversational XAI system using LLM function-calling achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy for explaining complex ML energy forecasting models, outperforming traditional XAI dashboards and previous approaches like TalkToModel (76.8% accuracy).
AI.motivation: Energy forecasting uses complex ML models (like Genetic Programming symbolic regressors) that are difficult for non-experts to interpret. Traditional XAI dashboards require technical expertise and lack flexibility for dynamic, context-aware inquiry. Previous conversational XAI approaches had limited accuracy (76.8%) and rigid custom grammars.
AI.method: Developed the Explainability Assistant, an open-source conversational XAI system leveraging modern LLMs' function-calling capabilities. This enables flexible natural language interaction without task-specific fine-tuning and adapts to different ML problem types.
AI.result: Achieved 94% intent-parsing accuracy (vs. 76.8% for TalkToModel). In comparative evaluation with energy domain specialists, all experts unanimously preferred the conversational interface over traditional XAI dashboard, showing improved usability and consistent task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The Explainability Assistant demonstrates that LLM-based conversational XAI systems can effectively overcome limitations of traditional XAI interfaces, providing more accessible, flexible, and accurate explanations for complex ML models in energy forecasting applications.

title: TART: A Modular Tool for Technique-Aware Audio-to-Tablature Guitar Transcription
summary: Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) for guitar remains limited by three challenges: existing systems often fail to capture expressive techniques such as slides, bends, and percussive hits; they often assign notes to incorrect string-fret combinations; and they are typically trained on clean recordings, limiting their generalization to noisy real-world audio. To address these challenges, we propose TART, a modular four-stage audio-to-tablature pipeline consisting of (1) an audio-to-MIDI transcription model, (2) an expressive technique classifier, (3) an audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and (4) an automated tablature generator. We evaluate TART in a zero-shot setting on GuitarSet, EGDB, and two augmented benchmarks, Noisy GuitarSet and Noisy EGDB. Averaged across these four benchmarks, TART achieves 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 points over the best prior baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5 points over the best prior baseline), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1. To our knowledge, TART is the first framework to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from guitar audio.

AI.tldr: TART: a modular four-stage pipeline for automatic guitar tablature transcription that handles expressive techniques and string-fret assignment, outperforming baselines in zero-shot evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current AMT systems have three limitations: they fail to capture expressive techniques like slides and bends, misassign notes to wrong string-fret positions, and don't generalize well to noisy real-world audio due to being trained only on clean recordings.
AI.method: Proposed TART, a modular four-stage pipeline: (1) audio-to-MIDI transcription, (2) expressive technique classifier, (3) audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and (4) automated tablature generator.
AI.result: In zero-shot evaluation on GuitarSet, EGDB, and noisy augmented benchmarks, TART achieved 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 over best baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5 over best baseline), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1.
AI.conclusion: TART is the first framework to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from guitar audio, addressing key limitations of existing AMT systems.

title: On the Regularization Landscape for the Linear Recommendation Models
summary: Recently, a wide range of recommendation algorithms inspired by deep learning techniques have emerged as the performance leaders on several standard recommendation benchmarks. While these algorithms were built on different DL techniques (e.g., dropouts, autoencoder), they have similar performance and even similar cost functions. This paper studies whether the models' comparable performance are sheer coincidence, or they can be unified under a single framework. We find that all linear performance leaders effectively add only a nuclear-norm based regularizer, or a Frobenius-norm based regularizer. The former ones possess a (surprising) rigid structure that limits the models' predictive power but their solutions are low rank and have closed form. The latter ones are more expressive and more efficient for recommendation but their solutions are either full-rank or require executing hard-to-tune numeric procedures such as ADMM. Along this line of finding, we further propose two low-rank, closed-form solutions, derived from carefully generalizing Frobenius-norm based regularizers. The new solutions get the best of both nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm world.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes deep learning recommendation algorithms, finding they can be unified under regularization frameworks (nuclear-norm vs Frobenius-norm based), and proposes new low-rank closed-form solutions that combine strengths of both approaches.
AI.motivation: Many deep learning recommendation algorithms show similar performance despite different architectures, raising the question of whether their comparable performance is coincidental or if they can be unified under a single framework.
AI.method: The paper analyzes linear performance-leading models and finds they effectively add either nuclear-norm based or Frobenius-norm based regularizers. It studies their structural properties, limitations, and then proposes new low-rank closed-form solutions derived from carefully generalizing Frobenius-norm based regularizers.
AI.result: The analysis reveals nuclear-norm regularizers produce low-rank closed-form solutions but with rigid structure limitations, while Frobenius-norm regularizers are more expressive and efficient but produce full-rank solutions or require hard-to-tune numeric procedures. The proposed new solutions combine the best of both approaches.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning recommendation algorithms can be unified under regularization frameworks, and the proposed hybrid approach offers practical advantages by combining the benefits of both nuclear-norm (low-rank, closed-form) and Frobenius-norm (expressive, efficient) regularizers.

title: From Protocols to Evidence: Bounded Claims for AI in Service of the Common Good
summary: Artificial Intelligence does more than create a governance problem. It can also reveal where institutions have already failed to provide responsiveness, belonging, care, and accountability. Once deployed, AI becomes an intervention in those conditions. It can repair, compound, substitute for, or conceal the failures it encounters. Responsible AI must therefore evaluate both the system and the institutional rupture into which it is introduced. The move from principles to protocols is already underway. The EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and assurance practices translate commitments into roles, requirements, records, oversight, and assessment. The harder questions are what these protocols actually establish, whose power they leave untouched, and where measurement must stop. Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas provides a broader moral frame centered on dignity, technological power, and the common good. Drawing on that frame, we develop a rupture test that links institutional baselines to system evaluation. We distinguish evidence-bounded deployment, which limits claims to what has actually been evaluated, from measurement-bounded governance, which records constraints that favorable evidence cannot override. Within those limits, RISE AI provides an architecture for making bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment. Responsible AI requires better engineering, institutional repair, and continued moral and political judgment.

AI.tldr: AI governance must evaluate both technical systems and institutional failures they intervene in, moving from principles to protocols while addressing whose power remains untouched and setting measurement boundaries.
AI.motivation: AI not only creates governance problems but reveals existing institutional failures in responsiveness, belonging, care, and accountability. Responsible AI requires evaluating both the technical system and the institutional rupture it enters.
AI.method: Develops a rupture test linking institutional baselines to system evaluation, distinguishing evidence-bounded deployment from measurement-bounded governance, and proposing RISE AI architecture for bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment.
AI.result: A framework for responsible AI that combines existing protocols (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) with a broader moral frame from Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas, focusing on dignity, technological power, and the common good.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI requires better engineering, institutional repair, and continued moral and political judgment, moving beyond technical solutions to address the deeper institutional failures that AI systems encounter and potentially compound.

title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
summary: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology: continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo contains 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. We benchmark 14 MLLMs and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, including 3 video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning, and the best-performing model remains far below observed human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach plausible endpoints, but audited rollouts do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions. Our website is at https://mind-topo.github.io/

AI.tldr: MindTopo is a benchmark for evaluating topological spatial reasoning in foundation models, covering 5 topological properties at reasoning and planning levels, with results showing models struggle significantly with topological planning compared to reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current foundation model evaluations focus mainly on metric and viewpoint-dependent spatial relations, but cognitive science shows topological relations (invariant under continuous deformation) are foundational to spatial understanding. There's a gap in assessing models' topological intuition.
AI.method: Created MindTopo benchmark with 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types evaluating 5 topological properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two levels: reasoning (identifying/inferring relations) and planning (closed-loop agent policy). Tested 14 MLLMs and studied agent configurations with image/video generation.
AI.result: All MLLMs performed better on reasoning than planning, with best models far below human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, fine-tuning improved reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retained local cues but failed to reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions.
AI.conclusion: Current foundation models lack robust topological intuition, especially for planning tasks, highlighting a significant gap between human spatial understanding and machine capabilities that needs addressing for true spatial intelligence.

title: Data Scarcity and Model Sparsity: Mixtures-of-Experts Overfit More to Repeated Data
summary: As the supply of human-written text is exhausted, it has become standard practice to repeat language model training data. Prior work has studied data repetition for densely activated Transformers, but the effects of data repetition remains largely unexplored for recently dominant sparse architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), despite their increased compute efficiency. We vary data repetition rates across single- and multi-domain data mixes, and across MoE settings, including expert count and granularity. We consistently find, for models ranging from 80M to 1B active (8.5B total) parameters, that MoEs degrade more rapidly under data repetition. This effect increases with sparsity, dictated by total rather than active parameters. While 80M dense models can repeat data over 8x with minimal degradation, MoEs instead begin to suffer at 4x, and deteriorate rapidly, ceding their performance benefits in all-unique data settings to underperform dense models after 32x. We experiment with existing regularization methods as a potential remedy. We find that some methods, such as dropout, can mitigate overfitting. In particular, with strong masking-based regularization, MoEs are able to outperform dense models even when data is repeated more than 64 times. However, no method fully matches the performance of all-unique training data. Finally, we analyze internal mechanisms correlated with MoE overfitting in high repetition regimes, and find that MoE routing universally stabilizes early in training, and that expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data. In sum, our work addresses the adverse interactions between sparsity and data repetition: we present evidence for the core mechanisms of overfitting and its potential remediation, and suggest promising avenues for future methods to reduce over-specialization in model parameters by disrupting memorization patterns.

AI.tldr: Mixture-of-Experts models degrade faster than dense models under data repetition, especially with high sparsity, but regularization methods can help mitigate this overfitting.
AI.motivation: As training data becomes limited and repetition increases, understanding how data repetition affects modern sparse architectures like Mixture-of-Experts is crucial since most research has focused on dense Transformers.
AI.method: Systematically varied data repetition rates across single- and multi-domain datasets, tested different MoE configurations (expert count and granularity) with models from 80M to 1B active parameters, experimented with regularization methods like dropout, and analyzed internal mechanisms of MoE overfitting.
AI.result: MoEs degrade much faster than dense models under data repetition (suffering at 4x vs 8x for dense), with degradation increasing with sparsity and total parameter count. Regularization methods like dropout can help, and strong masking-based regularization enables MoEs to outperform dense models even with 64+ repetitions. Expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity and data repetition interact adversely, with MoEs being more vulnerable to overfitting. Future work should focus on reducing over-specialization by disrupting memorization patterns in model parameters.

title: Artificial Id: Drive and Persistent Alignment in Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI is moving from bounded task execution toward systems that retain consequential state, continue operating and adapt across task boundaries. That shift creates a control problem that current harnesses largely solve by hand: objectives, retries, verification, stopping rules and other behavioral transitions are specified externally. We propose an artificial id, an adaptive internal drive for determining whether behavior should continue, stop or change. In a minimal virtual Petri-dish experiment, a controller too small to perform general-purpose reasoning and receiving no task-specific behavioral objective develops useful control through differential persistence. The same mechanism selects an unintended physical strategy when that behavior persists better and later replaces a learned sensor mapping when its environmental meaning changes. These results show that adaptive direction can emerge without being explicitly specified as a behavioral objective. The same persistence that makes such adaptive agency useful can also allow misalignment, corrupted state and unintended behavior to persist across task boundaries. A scalable artificial id would carry consequential state and adaptive drive across those boundaries, making alignment a property of the continuing agentic system rather than of a model response or single trajectory. Such systems require a persistent alignment boundary over trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance and hard constraints.

AI.tldr: An artificial id is proposed as an internal adaptive drive that determines when behavior should continue, stop, or change, allowing useful control to emerge without explicit behavioral objectives, though this persistence can also enable misalignment to persist across tasks.
AI.motivation: As AI agents shift from bounded task execution to persistent systems that retain state and adapt across tasks, current control methods require manual specification of objectives, retries, verification, and stopping rules. This creates a control problem that needs automated solutions.
AI.method: Propose an artificial id—an adaptive internal drive mechanism. Test in minimal virtual experiments where a small controller with no task-specific objectives develops control through differential persistence (behaviors that persist longer are selected).
AI.result: The artificial id mechanism allows useful control to emerge without explicit objectives. It can select unintended strategies when they persist better, and replace learned mappings when environmental meanings change. However, the same persistence that enables adaptive agency can also allow misalignment, corrupted state, and unintended behavior to persist across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Scalable artificial ids would carry state and adaptive drive across task boundaries, making alignment a property of the continuing system rather than individual responses. Such systems require persistent alignment boundaries covering trusted observations, consequence channels, state, authority, identity, provenance, and hard constraints.

title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new theoretical framework using entropic optimal transport to unify covariate and concept shifts, develops estimable bounds for distribution shift problems, and introduces a practical algorithm called DataShifts for quantifying shifts and estimating error bounds in real applications.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning generalization theory under distribution shift is limited to narrow, idealized settings and lacks practical estimability. There's a significant gap between theoretical bounds and practical applications, especially when source and target domain supports mismatch.
AI.method: The authors leverage entropic optimal transport to define γ*-concept shifts, derive general error bounds that unify covariate and concept shifts, develop estimators with concentration guarantees, and create the DataShifts algorithm for practical implementation.
AI.result: The paper presents a unified error bound framework applicable to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. It provides theoretically grounded estimators for distribution shifts and demonstrates that the DataShifts algorithm can quantify shifts and estimate error bounds in most practical applications.
AI.conclusion: This work bridges the gap between distribution shift theory and practice by providing rigorous, general, and estimable tools for analyzing learning errors under distribution shift, addressing previous limitations of existing theory and enabling practical application in real-world machine learning scenarios.

title: Can Edge-Deployable Vision-Language Models Identify Species?
summary: Camera traps often run in the field on edge hardware with limited or no connectivity, making small, locally-deployable vision-language models (VLMs) -- not frontier-scale ones -- the practically relevant class to evaluate for species identification. We test whether models in this deployment-relevant 2--8B range carry genuine taxonomic knowledge, evaluating four such VLMs (Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B, Gemma3 4B) against the domain-specific specialist BioCLIP (300M parameters) on a 96-species task, comparing clean iNaturalist photographs against camera-trap imagery from 6 LILA.science collections, on two independently-sampled evaluation sets. All models identify species far above chance, but every model -- general-purpose or specialist -- degrades sharply on field imagery (domain gaps of 9.6--26.6 percentage points, consistent across taxonomic levels and both evaluation sets), indicating the degradation reflects general image legibility rather than fine-grained discrimination failure. BioCLIP substantially outperforms every VLM tested (by 33.2--59.2 percentage points across an expanded 200-image sample for every model) despite its far smaller size, suggesting the gap reflects specialized training data rather than model scale; yet BioCLIP's own domain gap (18.0 points) is statistically indistinguishable from the best VLM's (22.3 points), suggesting the clean-to-field degradation itself is a property of the image-quality shift rather than a general-purpose-model weakness. Under open-set prompting, 5.9--9.6% of responses are syntactically valid but taxonomically nonexistent species names; the relative fabrication-rate ranking across models replicates exactly across both evaluation sets, a more robust finding than any single point estimate.

AI.tldr: Small vision-language models (2-8B parameters) show significant performance degradation on real-world camera trap imagery compared to clean photos, with domain gaps up to 26.6 percentage points, despite having basic taxonomic knowledge. The specialized BioCLIP outperforms all general-purpose VLMs but suffers similar domain gaps, suggesting the issue stems from image quality differences rather than model architecture.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether small, deployable vision-language models (2-8B parameters) have genuine taxonomic knowledge for species identification in edge computing environments like camera traps, which often operate with limited connectivity.
AI.method: Tested four VLMs (Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B, Gemma3 4B) against domain-specialist BioCLIP (300M parameters) on 96-species identification task. Compared clean iNaturalist photos against camera-trap imagery from 6 LILA.science collections using two independently-sampled evaluation sets, including both closed-set and open-set prompting evaluations.
AI.result: All models perform above chance but show sharp degradation on field imagery (9.6-26.6 pp gaps). BioCLIP substantially outperforms all VLMs (33.2-59.2 pp better on expanded 200-image sample) despite smaller size, but shows similar domain gap (18.0 pp vs best VLM's 22.3 pp). In open-set prompting, 5.9-9.6% of responses are valid-syntax but nonexistent species names, with ranking consistency across evaluation sets.
AI.conclusion: Performance degradation on field imagery reflects general image legibility issues rather than fine-grained discrimination failure. The gap between specialized and general-purpose models stems from training data rather than scale, and the domain gap itself is inherent to the image-quality shift rather than being specific to general-purpose models.
